News.title: Boy, 6, dies suddenly after falling ill during football match as devastated mum pays tribute to ‘courageous’ son
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

'COURAGEOUS BOY' Boy, 6, dies suddenly after falling ill during football match as devastated mum pays tribute to ‘courageous’ son

A SIX-YEAR-OLD boy who died suddenly after falling ill while playing football.

Max Kuc died unexpectedly on December 15 last year after a match for North East Leeds FC and his mother has paid tribute to her “courageous boy”.

As a baby Max battled cancer and a liver transplant but despite facing severe health issues he never stopped loving football.

In a fundraiser for the local club, his mum Lucy said he lived a life of “joy and happiness”.





She added that he will be remembered for his “infectious smile, determination and boundless enthusiasm for the game”.

News.title: Argentina vows to ‘recover’ Falklands & put sanctions on oil firms as president doubles down on threat to take UK island
News.content:
'NO OTHER PATH' Argentina vows to ‘recover’ Falklands & put sanctions on oil firms as president doubles down on threat to take UK island

ARGENTINA’S President has vowed to “recover” the Falkland Islands, warning “there is no other path forward”.

In his claim to the contested territory, Javier Milei declared the UK was facing “multiple crises” that are “unlikely to be resolved” while “Argentina’s future is flourishing and will prevail”.



In a fiery televised speech, Milei insisted the islands are “nationally relevant” and a crucial part of Argentina’s “future”.

The Argentinian leader declared he will sign a decree to sanction any oil companies working off the islands, “under the British occupation”.



His bold remarks come after Donald Trump suggested he would not back the UK if Argentina invaded the archipelago, citing the lack of support in the war on Iran.

The US President, an ally of Milei, said: “I was there when they had the first war, that was a long time ago…



“You comported yourself very well, took it back very shortly. But it is a long way away.

“So, your country’s not doing well. Don’t forget you get a big percentage of your oil from the Strait of Hormuz and you weren’t there to help me.”



The islands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, are the subject of a major dispute between Britain and Argentina.

The two countries waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982, in which 907 people were killed – 649 Argentine soldiers, 255 British troops, and three civilians.

In 2013, residents voted overwhelmingly in favour of remaining a British Overseas Territory.

Of 1,517 votes cast in the referendum, 1,513 were in favour and only three against.

The US has formally recognised the UK’s de facto administration of the islands but has not taken a formal position on sovereignty.



Referring to Trump’s latest stance, Milei said: “The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come.”

In another swipe to the UK, the right-wing leader claimed the UK “failed to heed” the call of the United Nations to not take “unilateral actions” on the island.

He said: “For more than 50 years, the United Nations have been calling Argentina and the United Kingdom not to undertake unilateral actions on the territory of the islands until the dispute is resolved, including the use of its national resources.



“However, the United Kingdom has systematically failed to heed that call.”

The Sea Lion project – an oilfield off the coast of the Falklands owned by an Israeli and a British firm – is due to begin in the months, Milei said.

He added: “If we do not act swiftly in a few months, they will have the material capacity to access the oil that lies underneath our sea.

“Something that has never happened before.

“That means that our national claim is facing a clear and present danger, and requires a proportional response. We will not allow it.”



Prime Minister Andy Burnham has confirmed that he will honour Sir Keir Starmer‘s commitment to spend 3.5% of UK GDP on core defence by 2035.

But the US has called for further investment and slammed NATO for being a “paper tiger” and previously hinted at leaving the alliance altogether.

One of the bombshell options aimed at pressuring the UK included the Falklands.

News.title: Traffic chaos on major UK route after crane breaks down spilling oil across road – as drivers warned of long delays
News.content:
HEAVY DELAYS Traffic chaos on major UK route after crane breaks down spilling oil across road – as drivers warned of long delays

THE Dartford Tunnel closed after a 50-tonne crane broke down and started spilling oil across the road – sparking commuter chaos.

Drivers were warned of huge delays due after the HGV became stranded on the busy route in Dartford, Kent, yesterday evening.

The west tunnel slammed shut at around 6pm, while traffic officers were scrambled to assess the spillage.

All traffic was then diverted into the east crossing as motorists were warned of four miles of congestion.





The Junction 1a entry slip road near Dartford was also closed during the chaos.

National Highways said: “Officers and a specialist recovery team are on scene working to remove the stranded crane as quickly as possible.

“Once the crane has been cleared the oil spill will need to be treated before the tunnel can be safely re-opened to traffic.

“National Highways maintenance contractors are on scene already to commence this as soon as the crane has been cleared from the tunnel.



“Traffic is being diverted through the east (right) tunnel.

“This incident is causing long delays on approach and on local routes in the area.

“Currently, delays of 30 minutes are being reported on the northbound approach to the Dartford Tunnels with heavy congestion from J2 (A2).”

Vehicles are charged up to £8.40 to use the Dartford Crossing.



It opened in stages from 1963 and is widely considered part of the M25 motorway.

Since 2008, it has been free for all motorists between 10pm and 6am.

News.title: ‘Dangerous’ man filmed himself sexually assaulting woman & sent himself nude pics from her phone after she passed out
News.content:
BEHIND BARS ‘Dangerous’ man filmed himself sexually assaulting woman & sent himself nude pics from her phone after she passed out

A MAN who filmed himself sexually assaulting a woman and sent himself nude pictures from her phone after she passed out has been jailed.

Kenan Samuel, 28, invited the woman over for drinks along with a male friend on December 18, 2020.

In the early hours of the morning she went to bed and passed out, unable to consent

Samuel climbed into the bed with the victim and started sexually assaulting her while filming himself.





The victim later reported Samuel to the police and his phone was seized.

Officers also uncovered he had sent a nude photo of the woman to himself and deleted the message so she wouldn’t notice.

He was jailed for five years at Peterborough Crown Court on August 28.

Samuel admitted to assaulting a female by penetration with part of body / a thing, voyeurism, and causing a computer to perform function to secure / enable unauthorised access to a program / data.



DC Sally Muntane-Crane, who investigated, said: “Samuel is a dangerous man who took advantage of the victim when she was in a vulnerable state.

“He was also cunning, deleting the evidence he had sent himself a nude photo from the victim’s phone without her consent.

“I would like to praise the victim for reporting what happened, and for showing tremendous strength and bravery during the investigation.

“I hope it gives confidence to other victims to come forward, knowing they will be listened to, and the police and wider criminal justice system will do everything they can to get justice for them.”

News.title: Two survivors pulled ALIVE from Nepal tunnel after week as oxygen pumped in & walls blasted in bid to rescue 500 trapped
News.content:
TWO workers have been pulled alive from a tunnel in Nepal more than a week after catastrophic floods devastated the region.

The pair were freed from a hydropower tunnel in the Rasuwa district where they had been trapped for nine days.



Images show the men, covered in mud, being carried from the site by rescue crews.

At least 1,259 people were killed in flash floods that struck along the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, with more than 5,000 still missing.



The workers were rescued during an ongoing operation at the Trishuli 3A tunnel – where crews are pumping air into the site and draining water.

Astonishing footage shows one man being pulled along a rope from a dark hole in the ground by a team of rescue workers.



A second man holds his hands in prayer as he is lifted from beneath the rubble on a stretcher.

Sanjay Shah was the first to be freed and taken to the Nepal Army barracks in Trishuli.



Another worker, identified as Kabir Maharjan, was also recused from the tunnel.

It remains unclear if these are the two men shown in footage.

Rescue operations have been focused on the hydropower tunnels where authorities hope workers have survived due to air pockets.

At about 2am on Monday, a controlled blast was carried out at the Trishuli 3A hydropower site in an attempt to reach those trapped.

Nepal’s communication minister Bikram Timilsina said officials remain hopeful more will be recovered alive.



Large boulders and flood waters overwhelmed many of the tunnels, blocking off entrances and burying them deep in mud.

It took rescue crews six days to find the tunnels at the Trishuli facility.

But as emergency crews continued clearing debris from the entrance this morning, the voices of those trapped inside could be heard calling out.



Rescue teams reportedly shouted, “Don’t panic, we are rescuing you”, and those inside responded, “Okay”.

About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydro power projects in Nepal, with around 500 believed to be stuck in tunnels.

The torrent of floodwater, mud and debris destroyed most of the hydropower projects along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers.

It comes as Nepalese morgues are overwhelmed with the number of bodies arriving since.

Entire settlements were engulfed in mud leaving many with no chance of escape.

Horrifying galleries displaying mutilated bodies are growing day by day as authorities desperately try to help relatives identify loved ones.

Blood samples are now being taken from relatives of those still missing as authorities race to identify bodies recovered from the devastating floods.

POLICE PROBE Man, 41, arrested after ‘indecent exposure and assault’ involving woman and child

A MAN has been arrested after an alleged indecent exposure and assault involving a woman and a child.

The 41-year-old man was arrested yesterday after the incident in Leeds on Sunday and he remains in custody.

The incident occurred at around 7.30pm near on York Road in the Killingbeck area.

The woman and child were reportedly in a car.





Specialist officers from Leeds safeguarding are supporting the victims while enquiries continue.

A spokesperson for West Yorkshire Police said: “A man has been arrested over an indecent exposure and assault in Leeds.

“The 41-year-old man was arrested this afternoon in relation to an incident involving a woman and child in York Road on Sunday, 30 August.

“The man remains in custody and specialist officers from Leeds Safeguarding are carrying out enquiries and are continuing to support the victims.



“We would like to thank everyone who assisted in sharing the appeal and who contacted us with information.”

Elsewhere, officers from West Yorkshire Police arrested a man yesterday morning after an alleged indecent exposure on the canal towpath.

A 20-year-old man was arrested after officers received reports of a man indecently exposing himself and he

A concerned woman called the police at 7.20am yesterday and officers were on the scene near Leeds Dock within 20 minutes.

News.title: Red Arrows flight path today: Route map and transit times for Friday’s International Ayr Show – Festival of Flight 2026
News.content:
THE Red Arrows are the aerobatics display team of the RAF, having performed for millions across their 62 year history.

Here’s all you need to know about todays display at Scotland’s International Ayr Show – Festival of Flight 2026.

What is the Red Arrows route today?

The Red Arrows will take off from Glasgow Prestwick Airport at around 6.01pm and will fly over parts of Kimarnock, Muirkirk and New Cumnock.



They will then fly over Drongan before beginning the show at around 6.10pm.



They will perform for around 21 minutes and then head back to Prestwick, where they will complete their journey.

Here are the official, down-to-the-minute timings for today’s flight path:

6.01pm – Prestwick

6.03pm – South of Kilmarnock

6.05pm – North of Muirkirk

6.07pm – North East of New Cumnock

6.09pm – North West of Drongan

6.10pm – Ayr Display

6.31pm – Oversea

6.32pm – West of Troon

6.33pm – Prestwick

You can see a map of the planned route below, per the website Military Airshows:



Why are there only seven Red Arrows in 2026?

In a shake-up announced on Saturday, May 23, the Red Arrows are now performing with seven aircraft instead of the traditional nine for the majority of their displays in 2026.

Reducing the numbers cuts down engine wear and tear by a massive 22% over the season.

But the full nine-craft formation isn’t dead, and will still be brought back for state occasions and national flypasts.

The change has been brought in to help manage the team’s ageing Hawk T1 jets as they prepare to transition to newer types of aircraft.



An RAF spokesperson said: “The Red Arrows are the pride of the nation, known globally for their world-class precision, speed, and teamwork.

“The Red Arrows will fly in a nine-aircraft formation for HM The King’s Birthday Flypast and the 4th of July 250 Commemorations in the USA this year.

“For other displays, they will operate with seven aircraft, continuing to deliver high-quality, engaging displays at air shows and events across the UK, mainland Europe and further afield.”

News.title: Britain will go bankrupt under Burnham, warns Kemi Badenoch as she accuses PM of saying YES to every spending demand
News.content:
BRITAIN will go bankrupt under Andy Burnham’s leadership because he refuses to say no to colleagues asking for more funds, Tory leader Kemi Badenoch claimed yesterday.

She insisted that his first statement to the Commons as PM on Tuesday made his problem clear — despite turmoil on the money markets over his grip on public finances.



Probed on whether he will bankrupt the country, she said: “If you listen to his statement, I think the answer is ‘probably’, because he had so many requests for government spending, so many requests for taxpayers’ money.

“He didn’t say no to anything.



“If someone doesn’t know how to say no, then they will run out of money.

“The problem with socialism is they always run out of other people’s money, not their own.”

Meanwhile, senior Labour MP Dame Emily Thornberry said she expected taxes to rise at next month’s Budget.

She pointed to “huge strains” on the economy as Chancellor John Healey grapples with inflation, the Iran War and an estimated £14billion blow to finances owing to increases in the Government’s borrowing costs.

Economists believe an estimated £14billion has been wiped away from the Government’s financial cushion due to the hikes in borrowing costs.

Lord O’Neill, an ally of the PM, says the bond markets would welcome the Government tackling the “sacred cows” such as the triple lock or welfare costs to get on top of the public finances.

News.title: Farage senior aide filmed suggesting way to avoid donations law
News.content:
Nigel Farage's senior aide suggested a way to get around electoral law to secure a foreign donation of Â£500,000 for Reform UK, according to undercover filming broadcast by Channel 4.

Dan Jukes was filmed meeting a man posing as the British-based son of a rich American businessman.

Electoral law sets out that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.

In this instance, the son would be a permissible donor, his father would not be.

The undercover filming was done by a group called Verbatim Investigations, which was founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting. Channel 4 News say they have verified the material they were given and chose to broadcast.

Reform UK denies any wrongdoing and claims to have "been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign funded climate change activists".

The reporter posing as the son of the American donor is filmed raising a concern that his father wouldn't be able to directly donate to the party within the law.

Filmed standing outside a pub in Westminster, Jukes said "you do realise that you can do it?"

Channel 4 say Jukes was suggesting that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father.

"Actually that does strike me as a solution," Jukes continues.

He then claims they have done it several times before, in exchanges bleeped out but which appear to refer to other instances where this mechanism had been used before.

"That's one of the ways in which we do it," he is recorded as saying.

Reform UK have launched an internal investigation into Jukes. They would not confirm if he remained a party spokesperson.

Later, Channel 4 broadcast footage from a lunch in Clacton in Essex, with both the reporter posing as the UK-based son, and an actor â his supposed American father. Opposite them are both Dan Jukes and the Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Farage says "it's all above board" after the son has told him he has been in discussions with both Jukes and Reform's Head of Policy, James Orr about it for some time.

"I'll be the registered donor," the son says. "But then dad will send the money to me, and then as soon as that's done and all those conversations are had the money is available."

"Thank you. Well, both of you. Thank you," Farage is heard saying.

Orr is also now the subject of an internal Reform UK investigation.

News.title: Controversial Jackdaw gas field set to be approved in weeks, sources say
News.content:
The UK government is set to give the go-ahead for a controversial new gas field off the coast of Aberdeen, the BBC understands.

Approval for the Jackdaw project could come as soon as mid-September, just before Parliament breaks for party conference season, according to government and industry sources.

The gas field was approved by the former Conservative government in 2022 but was delayed by a legal ruling from a Scottish court, after environmental groups successfully argued that consent was given without fully considering the climate impact.

Jackdaw's owner says it will account for about 6% of UK gas production when at peak output while environmental groups say it will provide only 2%.

Campaigners launched legal challenges after Jackdaw was approved in 2022 and when the Rosebank oil field off Shetland was given the green light in 2023.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites.

A judge ruled that more detailed climate assessments had to be published, and these updated estimates were put out for consultation in July.

News.title: Girl group Katseye are missing two members, but their tour still dazzles
News.content:
They may have been two members down, but the pop group Katseye received a hero's welcome as they played their first full concert in the UK.

The audience erupted with screams even before the show began, as the band broadcast their music videos on the O2 Arena's big screens, and the noise barely dipped for the next three hours.

It was proof that Katseye have become pop's biggest property (they're currently the most-streamed act on YouTube UK) even while singers Manon Bannerman and Sophia Laforteza are on health-related hiatus.

The stage felt emptier without them, but their bandmates worked hard to fill the gaps, hyping up the crowd with a succession of bass-heavy pop anthems and jaw-dropping dance breaks.

"Are you happy to see us?" asked the band's youngest member, Yoonchae Jeong, as if the answer hadn't been obvious from the moment they appeared in a storm of laser lights and launched into the Brazilian funk workout of Hootie Frutti.

"I think you guys are our loudest crowd ever, literally," marvelled Megan Skiendiel.

"This crowd is unbelievable," added Lara Raj.

The concert was only the second date of the band's Wildworld tour - but fans already knew every twist and turn from social media.

There was even a cheer of relief when Daniela Avanzini survived a complicated lift in the dance routine for Gabriella. On the opening night, her dance partner dropped her., external

News.title: British army told to stop non-essential training exercises to save money
News.content:
The Army has been told to stop "non-essential" training exercises to save money, according to a defence source.

It will continue to train soldiers preparing to be deployed or on deployments - such as units sent to Estonia, the Falklands or Cyprus.

But units back in the UK and who are not preparing for a specific deployment have been told to cut back on collective training exercises due to financial pressures.

It comes as Prime Minister Andy Burnham faces pressure to increase spending on defence.

The government is increasing defence spending to 2.5% of national income by next year, but is under growing pressure to reach a target of 3% by the end of the decade.

A defence source said the plans mean not doing what he called "nice to have training" - like large live fire exercises and rehearsing platoon attacks in UK training areas like Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire and Sennybridge in Wales.

It is understood planned exercises that were due to take place that are now cancelled include one involving the Royal Tank Regiment conducting live fire drills in Wales and a separate exercise involving tanks and Apache helicopters.

This was not the choice of the army, the source said. The pause is expected to continue for most of this year.

Other specific training aimed at modernising the Army â such as practising drone and counter-drone warfare is expected to continue.

The Army says it is prioritising the training that has been informed by lessons learnt from the war in Ukraine, and is reviewing each request for training on a case-by-case basis.

Though the government is increasing defence spending, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) is still struggling to fund all its investment plans.

Much of the new money has been earmarked for specific capital projects, including new weapons programmes. The part of the MoD's budget for training is still under significant pressure.

An Army spokesperson said: "Our training continues and we are prioritising activity that contributes most directly to readiness, deployability and operational effectiveness.

"We are also investing Â£2bn to transform training for the British Army over the next 15 years."

On Wednesday during Prime Minister's Questions, the chairman of the Commons Defence Select Committee, Labour's Tan Singh Dhesi, warned it was imperative to invest in the armed forces and urged Burnham to commit to reaching 3% of GDP spend on defence by 2030.

The prime minister replied: "I've made that commitment very clear, and I have done for a considerable period of time."

The government's wavering over defence spending was part of the downfall of Burnham's predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer - with former Defence Secretary John Healey resigning his position in response to Sir Keir's plans on funding the armed forces.

Plans set out in the Defence Investment Plan (Dip) will see defence spending rise to 2.7% of GDP by 2027/28, but there are no firm details on how further increases will be achieved beyond that date.

The Treasury has consistently said the government will set out plans for reaching both 3% and 3.5% at the spending review, due to take place next year.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has urged the prime minister to "cut welfare spending and invest that money in our defence". The party says it would spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

"Faced with a choice between spending on military training and spending on benefits... Labour chooses more benefits," Tory shadow secretary of state for work and pensions Helen Whately said.

Clancy's lawyer asked the judge to remove a juror after the jury forewoman sent a court note saying one holdout would not follow the court's instructions on reasonable doubt.

News.title: I lost my savings after a job interview scam
News.content:
Jobseekers are being warned to be vigilant as scammers are targeting people on job listings websites to trick them into downloading bogus interview tools.

One victim was invited on LinkedIn by a fake recruiter to take part in a job interview process and downloaded a normal-looking document which turned out to be malicious software.

Within hours the hackers had drained his cryptocurrency accounts of Â£18,000 of savings and disappeared.

"It's a horrible feeling to be out a substantial amount - something I wouldn't wish on my worst enemy," the victim, who wanted to stay anonymous, said.

News.title: 'Miracle' eagle with broken wing spotted back above Scottish coast
News.content:
A sea eagle that confounded experts by surviving into adulthood with a badly broken wing has been spotted back in the skies above Scotland's west coast.

The bird was dubbed the Isle of Mull's "miracle eagle" by charity the RSPB after it fell from its nest as a chick during a storm in 2023.

Experts that monitor the island's sea eagle population did not expect the male chick to survive, but it has now been spotted three years on - soaring above the island with the distinctive kink in its wing clearly visible.

Retired RSPB officer Dave Sexton, whose has worked with the island's sea eagles for more than 20 years, described the sighting as "incredible".

News.title: 'Gromit was nearly a cat!': Secrets from 50 years of Aardman
News.content:
Gromit was almost a cat. Shaun the Sheep was nearly given a voice. And Chicken Run helped change the Oscars forever.

As Aardman Animations marks its 50th birthday, its creators have been sharing some of the surprising twists behind the rise of Bristol's best-known creative success story.

Founded by school friends Sir Peter Lord and Sir David Sproxton in 1976, Aardman has given us Morph, Wallace and Gromit, Shaun the Sheep and Chicken Run, the world's most successful stop-motion film.

But the journey from two teenagers "mucking about with plasticine" to an Oscar-winning animation powerhouse has often hinged on chance decisions, practical compromises and creative instinct.

Few examples are better than Gromit.

News.title: AI tools that take notes for GPs could miss vital information, study suggests
News.content:
The report concluded AI scribes can help with administrative work but more research needs to be done to understand how they work in specific healthcare settings and how their design supports both patients and clinicians.

It comes months after the BBC heard from doctors in the West Midlands, who said their workload had been significantly cut by using the transcription tool Heidi.

At one clinic in Dudley, the tool was credited with reducing a backlog of posting patient letters from six months to 14 days.

One of the key findings by the University of Edinburgh was that although AI tools can help capture what patients say, they can sometimes miss important aspects of consultations - such as facial expressions, gestures and emotional state.

The report said AI summaries tend to prioritise clinical information, which can come at the expense of the patients' stories and experiences of their illness.

It was also found that patients may be hesitant to reveal sensitive information - such as substance abuse, domestic abuse or mental health struggles - when they know the consultation is being recorded and processed by AI.

Researchers also highlighted that manual notetaking serves important functions for clinicians in their reasoning and reflection on what the patient has said.

Their report said using AI scribes could result in "cognitive offloading" for clinicians - which means the tools take on some of their mental effort.

This can have benefits, the report said, as clinicians can spent their efforts having more meaningful conversations with patients or concentrating on complex tasks.

However, it also said the tools can reduce memory recall and skill development and highlighted instances where clinicians do not recognise their own notes or remember the patient the next time they see them.

News.title: Anger as human poo and 'maggot-infested' food left behind at beauty spot
News.content:
Bronwyn Larry, head of communications for the park authority, said this was not the first instance of wardens discovering "abandoned 'wild camps'".

"It does seem to be increasing," she said.

"People come to the area to enjoy the beautiful scenery, the beautiful views, but now we are being faced with litter and it's disturbing that beautiful view."

She said the authority found the shift towards more fly-tipping "baffling" and said they were struggling to "figure out how to talk to people" about the issue.

"It's not just here, for our park, it does seem to be across the national parks. We are constantly putting out messaging around The Countryside Code, external, and the algorithm that we follow... that's what I see, for me it's second nature to take back what you go with."

Social media has previously been suggested as a reason for a rise in the issue, with tourists visiting the "Instagrammable" national park urged to research and respect the area.

But Lally said that, while "many influencers visit the area", "generally their messaging is around visiting responsibly" because "they want it to be nice too".

"So it's really difficult to understand where this change of attitude is coming from," she said.

News.title: Weekend heat for parts of UK before more rain next week
News.content:
Temperatures are on the rise again in time for the weekend with areas of the south experiencing 27C on Sunday.

However, before that, wet and windy conditions are in the Friday forecast for many across the northern half of the UK.

Low pressure systems continue to roll in from the Atlantic across the far north of the UK, affecting mostly northern and western Scotland.

Meanwhile, high pressure will block and weaken these fronts across the southern half of England and Wales, where drought conditions and hosepipe bans continue.

News.title: Schools to close early for A66 crash funeral
News.content:
Supt John Wrintmore from Cleveland Police said there was potential for traffic disruption and delays from 15:00 to 17:00 on Friday.

"This will affect areas of South Bank, Normanby Road through Teesville, Ormesby and Marton, and Acklam Road," he said.

"We are working closely with highways departments from the local authority, who are leading on the traffic management for this event, in order to minimise disruption.

"As with any significant gathering, we have plans in place to ensure public safety and security, which is line with our usual process."

A spokesperson for Redcar & Cleveland Borough Council said: "A number of schools in the South Bank area will close earlier than usual on Friday afternoon due to anticipated traffic congestion and transport disruption associated with a local funeral taking place in the area.

"The decision was made after careful consideration of the potential impact on home-to-school transport and the departure of pupils, staff and families at the end of the school day.

"Schools have worked with the Local Authority and transport providers to consider arrangements for pupils, including those who travel to and from specialist educational settings.

"We recognise that early closure may cause inconvenience for some parents and carers, and we thank them for their understanding and cooperation."

The decision comes after a vigil, for one of the young men who died, last week was followed by disorder in Haswell, County Durham, where a number of cars were set on fire.

The incident prompted criticism from MPs and police.

The Volkswagen Passat involved in the collision was being pursued by police until 10 seconds before the crash, according to the police watchdog.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said the Passat was believed to be using cloned registration plates.

A total of 27 people have been arrested as part of a wider police operation against organised crime, following the crash.

News.title: Reform UK promises £80bn cuts to public spending
News.content:
Jenrick is due to give a major speech to the conference on Saturday but speaking at a fringe event with journalist Allister Heath, he sought to reassure voters that Reform's policies would be affordable.

He said it was important to "learn the lessons of [former Prime Minister] Liz Truss" who he said "basically went into a sweetie shop, took everything off the shelves and stuck it into a budget".

"Quite rightly the markets reacted very negatively to that."

Jenrick was a health minister in 2022 when Truss's plan to deliver large energy bill subsidies and Â£45bn of tax cuts shook market confidence in the UK's financial credibility.

Reform has previously said it wanted to cut inheritance tax but Jenrick suggested that would not be a priority, arguing relatively few people were affected by it.

"It's a bold chancellor that would say I'd rather privilege 36,000 families than 40 million [income] taxpayers," he said.

He said his party would retain the triple lock - the mechanism which ensures pensions rise by either 2.5%, the rate of inflation or the rate of average earnings, whichever is highest.

The triple lock is estimated to cost Â£15.5bn per year by 2030 but Jenrick said he could not look pensioners "in the eye" and cut their income "while there is so much waste in the public sector".

He said it would be "fundamentally unfair going to pensions before we have made hard choices elsewhere".

Jenrick has written to investors who hold government debt to set up meetings in London and New York to discuss what fiscal rules he would set with the aim of reducing the cost of borrowing.

The past few days have seen global borrowing costs rise, with the UK's costs increasing to a 28-year high.

Also speaking at the conference, the party's business spokesman Richard Tice set out a number of proposals aimed at increasing house building on brownfield sites - land that has previously been built on.

He said the party would consult on measures including scrapping stamp duty, capital gains tax and tax on rental income for a decade for homes built on brownfield sites.

Under the proposals, affordable housing requirements would be removed for brownfield developments outside major cities.

The party's policy document says its plans would reduce tax receipts but argued that additional homes built as a result would boost the economy.

Tice has also suggested cutting business rates for high street shops, offsetting the cost by increasing the tax for online retailers.

Reform's conference at the Birmingham NEC comes at the end of a turbulent summer which saw its leader Nigel Farage resign and then re-run in his Clacton constituency in a bid to end questions about a Â£5m gift he received before becoming an MP.

There is also a police investigation into donations made to the party.

The main business of the conference is expected to take place on Friday and Saturday, with speeches from Farage and other senior figures, as well as an address by the leader of the French far right National Rally party, Jordan Bardella.

News.title: Households warned gas price spike could pile fresh pressure on energy bills
News.content:
Households across the UK are being warned to brace for higher energy bills this winter as European countries scramble to replenish their natural gas stores before the weather dips.

Wholesale natural gas prices are already at three-year highs, which could lead to increased energy bills for businesses and consumers.

Europe, which delayed its summer stockpiling due to high wholesale costs sparked by the Iran war, had been gambling the conflict would end before winter and prices would in turn fall.

Storage levels are significantly lower than usual for this time of year, with countries facing the prospect of rushing to buy gas now or paying potentially higher prices when the winter comes.

The European benchmark natural gas price topped â¬75/MWh on Wednesday, its highest level since late 2022, the tail end of a spike caused by Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Natural gas prices in the UK this week topped 185p per therm, also the highest since late 2022.

The price has jumped in the past week amid a return to hostilities between the US and Iran, with analysts fearing the renewed fighting will keep the key Strait of Hormuz closed even longer. Typically, around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) is transported through the waterway.

Hamad Hussain, senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, said he did not expect the waterway to begin reopening until early 2027.

Even then, there will be a lag before energy is flowing freely through the strait and pressure on energy prices are eased.

"The risks to gas prices are definitely tilted towards the upside," Hussain told the BBC, warning that the gas price would top â¬80 by the end of this year.

Hussain recalled interviews with gas storage operators at the outbreak of the US-Israeli war in Iran saying they would wait three to four months for the crisis to ease before stocking up.

"We are about six months into the strait being effectively closed and that obviously has not happened," he added.

Higher wholesale gas prices feed through to household energy bills by helping determine regulator Ofgem's price cap.

The energy price cap rose in July, and will increase by 4% in October, leaving a typical household paying Â£1,723. But analysts at the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight have forecast domestic energy prices could rise a further 9% in the new year, bringing renewed concern to households during the coldest months.

Dr Craig Lowrey, principal consultant at Cornwall Insight, told the BBC on Thursday a fresh increase in wholesale prices would "increase pressure on our January price cap forecast".

However, he cautioned that there was "plenty of time to go" and a fall in wholesale prices could ease the pressure.

News.title: Badenoch accuses Burnham of kicking defence spending into the long grass
News.content:
Badenoch repeated existing Conservative plans to fund an increase in defence spending, including by reimposing the two-child benefit cap.

The cap, which was scrapped by Labour in April, meant parents could only claim universal credit or tax credits for their first two children.

She said the final part of her party's plans to reach the 3% spending figure on defence had now been completed.

The Tories said this would include saving at least Â£4bn through reforms to housing benefit and removing the VAT exemption for Motability vehicles, saving Â£1bn.

"Alongside savings from the disastrous Chagos deal and re-purposing money from the British Business Bank into defence, we will be able to hit that 3% target," Badenoch said.

Housing benefit made up about 12% of the government's welfare bill this year, with Â£37.3bn forecast to be spent.

The Motability scheme, operated by a private company overseen by a charity, has historically given disabled people in receipt of eligible welfare benefits a 20% VAT discount on cars.

Last year, Rachel Reeves made the first changes to the Motability scheme in 50 years, removing about 50,000 premium cars like BMWs and Mercedes from the scheme and reinstating 20% VAT for most new cars, along with higher mileage charges.

Challenged over whether she was increasing child poverty to fund defence by reimposing the two-child benefit cap, Badenoch denied this.

"It is not going to increase child poverty. What increases child poverty is children's parents not having work or being paid low wages. We want to grow our economy," she told the BBC.

"Right now there are some people making choices not to have children because they can't afford it and paying for other people to have more children. That is not fair."

Responding to Badenoch's speech, a Labour Party spokesperson said: "These unserious plans are hardly surprising from the same Tory Party that hollowed out our Armed Forces, shrinking the British Army to its smallest size since the Napoleonic era.

"Andy Burnham has made it clear that his Labour government is determined to give our Armed Forces the investment needed to keep us safe.

"In just two years, Labour has delivered the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War, with funding already higher than at any point during 14 years of Conservative government."

It comes after Badenoch pressed Burnham over the issue during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, when she urged him to cut welfare spending and invest the money in defence.

Burnham also came under friendly fire from Labour MP Tan Dhesi at PMQs, who called on the prime minister to urgently commit to setting out a path to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

"Defence is definitely one area where vibes alone just isn't going to be enough," he said.

Burnham has insisted his government is committed to fully funding its defence plans, saying it will set out a pathway to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 in the spring.

News.title: Burnham and Macron agree to scale up action on small boats
News.content:
Macron said: "This is a very strong relationship. For me it is extremely important, and I'm here with willingness and a commitment to get closer."

The French leader's visit to the UK was primarily to mark the Bayeux Tapestry's loan to the British Museum. He met King Charles at the museum on Wednesday, ahead of the medieval tapestry going on public display next week.

In bilateral talks on Thursday, No 10 said Burnham and Macron agreed they were making headway in reducing small boat crossings in the English Channel but now needed to go further.

They also "discussed the UK's drive to get closer to Europe", while Burnham raised concerns about the potential impact of the Made in Europe procurement plan, being drawn up in Brussels to protect EU industries, on British sectors.

Burnham has previously called for closer ties with Europe, as had his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

The pair also discussed establishing local assembly lines in Ukraine for the Scalp long-range missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile.

The leaders also discussed the situation in the Middle East and the need to ensure de-escalation in the Strait of Hormuz.

And Burnham raised Israel's move to open up tenders for the construction of settlement homes in a strategically important part of the occupied West Bank, saying it was "unacceptable and only served to undermine the prospect of the two-state solution".

The development in the so-called E1 area would in effect divide the West Bank in two and isolate East Jerusalem.

Plans to build there have long been internationally condemned, with settlements illegal under international law.

The arrival of the first foreign leader under the Burnham premiership is an important symbolic moment - it shows the relationship with Paris is an important priority.

But it also reflects an obvious reality - to further reduce small boats crossings, working with France will be essential.

France and the UK have been working extremely closely on Ukraine and Iran, trying to jointly influence the White House.

And Paris will be an important player as the UK seeks even stronger economic ties with Europe under the new No 10 administration.

The "mega dinghies" crossing the Channel illegally - first seen earlier in August with a 15-metre long vessel carrying a record 230 migrants towards the UK - are arguably the most pressing challenge facing the pair.

It follows a summer when the number of small boat arrivals in the UK fell to a seven-year low.

News.title: Police release bodycam after teen allegedly claimed a ‘demon’ ordered girlfriend’s murder
News.content:

A chilling 37-minute police bodycam video released Thursday captures the gruesome moment officers discovered the body of a Pennsylvania college student hidden inside her own vehicle — a brutal killing her teenage boyfriend blamed on a "demon," court records show.

Royce Moser, 18, of North Strabane Township, stands charged with criminal homicide in the death of Karoline Heintz, a student at PennWest California University. His 56-year-old mother, Rachel Moser, is accused of helping orchestrate a twisted cover-up to shield her son.

According to a criminal complaint, Heintz’s father raised the alarm when she failed to return to campus, tracking her location via an Apple AirTag inside her Jeep. Police located the vehicle in a campus parking lot, where the footage shows an officer peering through the dark glass with a flashlight before shouting for backup.

open image in gallery Police body cam footage released by the California Borough Police Department in Washington County, Pennsylvania shows first responders working a scene after police officers discovered the body of a college student in a vehicle

"Control, I need EMS here right now," the officer frantically radioed. "I’ve got an unconscious female in the back of this car right now... I've got blood everywhere."

After smashing two windows to reach the victim, officers confirmed the horrific scene.

In a police affidavit, investigators detail how Royce Moser allegedly snapped during an argument in his driveway, telling Heintz to wait before grabbing a knife from inside his home.

Moser told police a "demon took over" and instructed him to stab the young woman. After the attack, Moser shoved Heintz's body into the rear hatch, took the wheel, and had his mother follow him to the university to dump the vehicle, according to authorities.

open image in gallery In a police affidavit, investigators detail how Royce Moser allegedly snapped during an argument in his driveway, telling Heintz to wait before grabbing a knife from inside his home

State police say the cover-up didn't end there. Investigators allege Rachel Moser brought her son to her Beallsville home, ordered him to bathe, threw his bloody clothes in the washing machine, and stuffed the murder weapon into a trash bag. Police later recovered the knife after executing a search warrant.

Both mother and son face charges of tampering with evidence, abuse of a corpse, and obstruction of justice. Rachel Moser faces additional counts including hindering apprehension.

Defense counsel for Royce Moser declined to comment, while a representative for Rachel Moser did not immediately return requests for comment.

The mother-son duo are being held without bail at the Washington County Jail ahead of an Oct. 13 formal arraignment.

"This is a parent’s worst nightmare," Heintz's family said in a statement. "Karoline was loved by all. She was a kind, smart, beautiful girl. We want justice for our 'sweet' Karoline."

Amy Hunt will continue her busy summer as the only athlete running both the women’s 100m and 200m at the Diamond League Final in Brussels this weekend.

The young British sprint star – who won a silver medal at the Commonwealth Games five weeks ago, claimed a record four gold medals at the European Athletics Championships shortly after and has since competed in Diamond League events in Zurich and Lausanne as well as a meeting in Brescia – will face two stacked fields at the King Baudouin Stadium, with Olympic silver medallist Sha’Carri Richardson, World Championship silver medallist Tina Clayton and Commonwealth Games champion Zoe Hobbs headlining the 100m field, and two-time Olympic medallist Julien Alfred the favourite in the 200m.

There are global superstars littered throughout the events as the season-long Diamond League reaches its conclusion, with unbeatable pole vault icon Mondo Duplantis finally having a legitimate rival in the form of Emmanouil Karalis, making for a fascinating Friday night showdown, while Audrey Werro vs the ever-improving Femke Broeders-Bol will be a blockbuster 800m match-up in the penultimate race of the meeting on Saturday evening.

Recent world-record breakers Alison Dos Santos (men’s 400m hurdles) and Masai Russell (women’s 100m hurdles) will both be in action once more, while the likes of Georgia Hunter Bell in the women’s 1500m, Matthew Hudson-Smith in the men’s 400m and Ben Pattison in the men’s 800m provide further British interest. In addition to the Diamond Trophy, there is an extra incentive for the winners, with automatic qualification for the lucrative World Athletics Ultimate Championship later this month on the line.

Here’s everything you need to know about the event:

When is the Diamond League Final?

The Diamond League Final will take place over two nights on Friday 4 September and Saturday 5 September at the King Baudouin Stadium in Brussels, Belgium.

Amy Hunt has become the queen of British sprinting and will look to makes waves at the Diamond League final ( Reuters )

How can I watch it?

The BBC has the United Kingdom television rights to every Diamond League meeting, with live coverage of the first night of the Diamond League Final available on BBC Three from 7pm BST on Friday 4 September and the second night of action available on BBC Two from 7pm BST on Saturday 5 September. Both nights will also be shown on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website.

Two Palestinian teenagers have been shot dead in the West Bank as the military razed an entire village near Hebron in the latest escalation of violence in the occupied territory.

Khalil Abu Alia, 16, a high school student, and Omar al-Nassan, 19, were shot after a group of settlers under police and army escort entered the al-Mughayyir village near Ramallah on Wednesday to take sheep from a Palestinian home, local residents said.

The army claimed its troops were providing ​security to police officers and Israeli settlers who had gone to take sheep claimed by them. The military offered no evidence of ownership of the livestock.

Snipers climbed on rooftops and shot Abu Alia while he was on the doorstep of his house, his teacher Waheed Abu Naim told the Guardian.

They also shot Al-Nassan twice, the second time in the back, the villagers said. Both died before they could reach hospital.

Abu Alia was killed by a soldier but it wasn’t clear whether Al-Nassan was shot by a soldier or a settler, the paper reported.

The Israeli army claimed its soldiers fired on "key instigators" of a “violent disturbance”, apparently referring to an attempt by the Palestinians to resist the settlers by throwing stones and cinder blocks.

A person waves Palestinian flags during the funeral procession for two teenagers killed by Israelis at Al-Mughayyir village in occupied West Bank on 3 September 2026 ( Reuters )

The killings at al-Mughayyir come amid intensifying settler violence in the West Bank, where a siege by settlers of Qusra village in August drew international condemnation.

At least 79 Palestinians, including 19 children, have been killed in the West Bank by Jewish settlers or Israeli forces since the beginning of 2026, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.

Israeli soldiers and settlers had previously killed three students from the al-Mughayyir boys school, where Abu Alia was due to start his grade 11, Mr Abu Naim, who taught all five boys killed in recent weeks, said. “We don’t know how long these crimes are going to continue,” he told the Guardian. “This week we are making extra security preparations for the new semester which starts in three days."

The Benjamin Netanyahu government has spearheaded a ​rapid expansion of Jewish ​settlements in the West Bank, which was captured by Israel in the 1967 war, establishing dozens ​of new settlements and settler outposts.

Rights ⁠groups say the increasing settler presence on the edge of Palestinian villages, like Qusra, is part of a wider effort to seize more land from Palestinians, ​further eating into territory where Palestinians aim to establish a state.

The latest killings of the Palestinian teenagers came after foreign secretary Ed Miliband stated on Tuesday that the UK would “reset” its policy on Israel in the coming weeks, as one of his ministers suggested goods coming out of Israeli settlements in the West Bank could be subject to sanctions.

The UN general assembly is due to vote on a resolution calling for the world to move away from the traditional Mercator map, which shrinks the size of Africa and exaggerates northern landmasses, in favour of designs that more accurately reflect the true size of countries.

The draft resolution asks governments, schools, international organisations, and technology companies to adopt the Equal Earth projection and other equal-area maps wherever the true scale of continents matters, with the aim of establishing more proportionally accurate maps as a new global norm. It does not seek to ban the Mercator projection outright.

The vote is set for Friday.

The Mercator projection, which is currently used worldwide, increases distortion the further a region sits from the equator. Since Africa straddles the equator, it seems comparatively smaller than its actual size, while Europe, North America, Greenland, and Russia all appear substantially larger than they are.

As a result, Africa, along with Latin America, India and other equatorial regions, appear much smaller relative to northern countries than their true area. The map, for example, depicts Africa as similar in size to Greenland, despite the continent being 14 times larger than the Danish territory.

The UN resolution was brought by Togo with the African Union’s backing, Togo's foreign minister Robert Dussey said. He did not specify the total number of nations that were supporting the vote.

In a briefing to the African Group at the UN this week, he said the importance of the issue went beyond geography.

"A map is never neutral," Mr Dussey reasoned. “It shapes perceptions, influences how the place of peoples and continents in the world is understood, and may, sometimes from the earliest years of schooling, perpetuate representations that do not correspond to geographic reality."

"Africa is not asking for preferential treatment," he said. "Africa is asking that its reality, aspirations and contribution to the international system be duly taken into account."

open image in gallery Mercator projection of the Earth ( Nasa )

He urged African delegations to broaden support for the resolution before Friday's vote, which he described as a test of the continent's ability to act with one voice at the UN.

Togo hosted a reception for all UN member states on the eve of the vote as part of that push.

Mr Dussey said he was aiming for as broad a consensus as possible when asked if he expected opposition to the resolution.

"I'm an academic before a politician," he said. "As an academic, I say we have to have as large a consensus as possible, because we are here at the UN, we never know.”

A petition on the fundraising platform Change for the campaign, called #CorrectTheMap, had gathered around 11,000 signatures ahead of the vote. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August 2025 and asked Togo to lead the push for its adoption at the UN.

“As Africa becomes increasingly central to solving global challenges,” the petition says, “it is critical to represent its true scale.”

open image in gallery The Correct the Map campaign wants the Equal Earth projection adopted in place of Mercator ( EqualEarth )

Historians and geographers have long argued that the Mercator map reflects Western assumptions about the world, and some campaigners have used the term "cartographic colonialism" to denounce what they have described as its negative effects.

German historian Arno Peters was one of the most prominent critics of the projection, launching an alternative map based on the Gall-Peters projection in 1973. Togo's campaign is instead promoting the 2018 Equal Earth map, developed by an international team of cartographers, which supporters say offers a more accurate representation of the size of every continent.

Mr Dussey connected the map campaign to another African Union-backed resolution passed at the UN in March which described the transatlantic slave trade as the "gravest crime against humanity" and was approved by 123 states, with three against and 52 abstentions.

If the resolution passes, Togo's government will hold an event in the capital, Lomé, with Unesco, the African Union, and technology companies including Google Maps in the first quarter of next year to work out how the change may be implemented.

In a world first, a man has lived without dialysis for nine months after receiving a genetically modified pig kidney.

Tim Andrews, 66, from New Hampshire, suffered end-stage kidney failure brought on by type 2 diabetes before undergoing the pioneer procedure in the US in January 2025.

Doctors explained that the animal organ, taken from a Yucatan miniature pig and genetically engineered for compatibility with the human immune system, served as a temporary "bridge" while Mr Andrews awaited a transplant from a human donor.

He lived successfully with the genetically edited organ for 271 days before transitioning to a short period of dialysis and subsequently receiving a donor human kidney.

Medical teams said the milestone marks the longest recorded dialysis-free survival following a pig kidney transplant in a living patient, and the first successful transition from pig-to-human kidney transplantation.

It was transplanted in January last year and began working immediately.

open image in gallery Medical teams said the milestone marks the longest recorded dialysis-free survival following a pig kidney transplant in a living patient ( PA )

After roughly six months, damage developed in the kidney’s blood vessels which progressed to organ failure and the pig kidney was removed.

Mr Andrews later received a kidney from a dead human donor.

In a CNN documentary, he said the pig kidney transplant was a “miracle”, adding: “I was alive, and I hadn’t been in a long time.”

He said he was able to cook, vacuum and take long walks with his dog Cupcake.

Researchers said no pig viruses or other pig pathogens were detected at any point.

They added that the findings support pig kidney transplantation as potentially a bridge for people facing long waits for a human kidney, while highlighting the need for further research.

The team, from Mass General Brigham academic centres and hospitals in the US, published their findings in the Lancet medical journal.

Lead author Dr Leonardo Riella, from the centre for transplantation sciences at Mass General Brigham, said: “The organ shortage is the greatest crisis we have right now in transplantation.

“We know that the best treatment option for patients with end-stage kidney disease who have developed renal failure is transplantation, but we simply don’t have enough human organs to transplant in a timely manner.

“Our vision is that xenotransplantation could help address this gap – initially as a bridge to get patients off dialysis while they wait for a human donor kidney, and potentially, as we establish long-term safety and durability, as a destination therapy in its own right.”

open image in gallery Mr Andrews lived successfully with the genetically edited organ for 271 days before moving to short-term dialysis and receiving a donor human kidney ( PA )

He added: “The patients are the true pioneers here. By stepping forward and being willing to participate in these early-stage studies, they are advancing the science.

“Without their trust and courage, we would not be able to do what we do.”

Another pig kidney transplant to a living human was undertaken in 2024 at Massachusetts General Hospital, where the patient survived 52 days before dying from heart issues unrelated to the transplant.

Dr Rommel Ravanan, chief medical officer for NHS Blood and Transplant in the UK, who is a consultant nephrologist, said the US and China have reported several similar transplants since 2022.

There are currently no clinical trials in the UK for a similar procedure although regulators have looked into how they would work.

He told the Press Association: “Advances in genetics technology enable teams to ‘knock out’ some of the pig genes, so the human body is less able to recognise the organ was different.

“Recent improvements in genetic mapping and the development of techniques such as CRISPR ‘genetic scissors’ have made this more possible.

“Pigs are chosen for several reasons, including that their organ size and anatomy is similar to that of human.

“Public surveys have shown most, but not all, people in the UK are supportive of the idea of lifesaving animal to human transplants.

“People are even more supportive when told animal to human transplants should only be introduced if shown to be safe and effective.

“It’s important to recognise that, even if shown to be effective, there is still a very long way to go before these kinds of transplants could become an everyday reality.

“With the transplant waiting list at an all-time high, and people dying on the transplant waiting list every day, there is an urgent need for more people to support organ donation by joining the NHS Organ Donor Register and talking to their family about their wish to be an organ donor.”

Dr Ravanan said a Department of Health and Social Care-sponsored advisory group of experts has made recommendations to ministers on the UK’s response to pig organ transplants, which were accepted.

“These recommendations cover policy in this field, including regulation, oversight, ethics including animal welfare, and research.”

The new hosts of The Grand Tour have been approved by former stars Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May, all of whom gave the incoming motorheads advice ahead of filming.

Replacing former presenters are social media star and train enthusiast Francis Bourgeois, as well as YouTubers Thomas Holland and James Engelsman, best known for their motoring channel Throttle House. It’s fair to say they have big shoes to fill.

“They’ve been very supportive, very warm, very open in just saying, ‘Go ahead – make it your own,’ even though we have been sensitive in honouring what the show is all about, and keeping car enthusiasm central,” Bourgeouis tells The Independent, days before the new season’s premiere on Prime Video this Friday (4 September).

open image in gallery Thomas Holland, Francis Bourgeous and James Engelsman are ushering in new era for ‘The Grand Tour’ ( Prime Video )

May had a more hands-off approach – and it was effective in its simplicity. “His sentiment was, ‘Don’t ask me – just do your thing,’” Holland explains. “It was the right thing to hear. It was like Yoda.”

Holland has admitted that “there was a lot of trepidation and fear” when he was first approached about becoming one of the new hosts, and was left wondering: “Do I do this?” But he also knew it didn’t matter what he was thinking: “Obviously I was going to do it”. He also addressed concerns any fans might have about this new era of the show, urging them to “give it a go”.

Nobody’s more surprised he’s the new host of The Grand Tour than “train guy” Bourgeois, who gained widespread popularity for his infectiously enthusiastic videos about trainspotting, which would often go viral on TikTok and Instagram. Five years ago, if you’d told him he’d be replacing Clarkson and co as host of the motoring show, he “would have considered what kind of mushrooms were on my al funghi pizza”.

His casting on the show was backed by his co-hosts thanks to his extremely niche car knowledge. “It was a huge green flag early on,” Engelsman says. “We all had the same reaction – ‘but he’s the train guy.’ But he’s also the car guy.” (Bourgeois worked for six months as a mechanical engineer at Rolls-Royce.)

open image in gallery New ‘Grand Tour’ host’ Francis Bourgeois – not just ‘the train guy’ ( Prime Video )

Holland, who is originally from Canada and studied biology, founded Throttle House in 2015 “out of boredom”. The channel initially focused on BMW builds and occasional car reviews, but began to gain momentum when Engelsman joined in 2018.

Engelsman, who is from the UK, became part of Throttle House after suggesting ideas to Holland and asking to be part of his videos. The duo had their first meeting in person at a gathering of Miata car owners.

Of the new trio, Bourgeois is arguably the most famous, having amassed millions of followers and celebrity fans for his trainspotting videos.

The 24-year-old, real name Luke Nicolson, gained widespread popularity for his infectiously enthusiastic videos about trainspotting, which would often go viral on TikTok and Instagram, and even featured cameos from singer Joe Jonas and the Prince and Princess of Wales.

open image in gallery YouTube stars Thomas Holland and James Engelsman are bringing their car camaraderie to motoring show ( Prime Video )

Beyond social media, Bourgeois has ventured into modelling, collaborating with brands including Gucci and The North Face, and has authored a book titled The Trainspotter's Notebook. He also hosted the Channel 4 digital series Trainspotting with Francis Bourgeois, which featured appearances from footballer Jesse Lingard and musicians Sam Ryder and AJ Tracey.

The Grand Tour races back to screens on Friday (4 September).

News.content:

Nick Kyrgios has accepted a one-month suspension after testing positive for cocaine, the International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) said.

The Australian, 31, failed a drugs test during an ATP Tour event in Mallorca in June 2026. The former Wimbledon finalist was provisionally suspended last month.

The ITIA said Kyrgios had agreed to attend a treatment programme approved by the ITIA, which has lowered Kyrgios’ suspension from three months to one month.

As a result, Kyrgios’ suspension is already over, as the ITIA said his provisional ban began on 4 August 2026 and ended on 3 September 2026.

The ITIA said Kyrgios’ explanatation that he had used cocaine “socially during a night out” was “consistent with the level of cocaine found in his sample”.

As a result, the ITIA accepted his use of cocaine was outside of competition and subject to a lighter penalty.

After his provisional suspension was announced last month, Kyrgios said he had made “a huge mistake”.

He wrote on Instagram: “I wanted you to hear this from me first. I recently failed a drug test in Mallorca after testing positive for cocaine.

“I made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it. I’m sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me. Above all, I’m sorry to the kids who follow me.

“I know the example this sets and I’m deeply disappointed in myself.”

His first-round loss to fellow Australian Adam Walton in Majorca was his last competitive singles outing and one of only four singles matches he has played this season.

Kyrgios’ career has been blighted by knee and wrist problems since his run to the Wimbledon showpiece in 2022 and his ranking has slipped to 919 in the world.

He said he would not make “excuses” for the positive test but cited the toll of his physical issues.

“My body hasn’t been able to do what my mind expects it do, and coming to terms with being near the end of my career has been harder than I ever imagined,” he said.

“At times I’ve felt hopeless and alone. However, the good news is that this has given me a wake-up call.”

Kyrgios added he would be taking a 28-day break from social media to focus on “getting myself right”, concluding: “I’m sorry, I’ll come back better.”

Britain’s Dan Evans was banned for a year for taking cocaine out of competition in 2017 but the rules changed in 2021, with the penalties reduced.
