World.title: What do Spain’s migrant crisis and Germany’s knife-edge election mean for Europe?
World.content:
The Spanish exclave of Ceuta on the North African coast is struggling to deal with a surge of unauthorized migrants. Over 70,000 arrived in a mass crossing from Morocco at the end of July, and although the numbers have fallen since then, police and the authorities are struggling with outbreaks of violence and criminality. Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has faced protests in cities across the country, and the crisis poses a challenge for the European Union’s borders. Host Anne McElvoy talks to Tim Röhn, Senior Editor of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, who has reported extensively from Ceuta for POLITICO.

Also on the podcast, could the far-right be on the verge of an electoral breakthrough in Germany? This weekend’s election in the Eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt could result in the Alternative for Germany forming a government, the first time a far-right party has tasted power since the Second World War. Anne has been on the road in the state, writing about how two chancellors, Merz and Merkel, have lost the old East. She’s joined by Josef Forster, BILD’s politics editor, on what might follow for Germany’s leadership.

World.title: Friedrich Merz will lose Sunday’s regional election — whatever the result
World.content:
But the other likely outcomes offer little relief for Merz.

If the AfD falls short of a governing majority in the state — an outcome that appears increasingly likely based on the latest polling — Merz’s second-place Christian Democratic Union will face a series of untenable choices as it tries to cobble together a coalition with left-wing parties. Any such alliance would likely be doomed from the outset, while remaining dependent on far-left or far-right support to pass legislation.

Concerns are also mounting that the AfD may be preparing for this scenario by challenging the outcome of Sunday’s election. The party has already issued press releases casting doubt on mail-in ballots, while its lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, has voiced similar concerns on social media.

Whatever the result on Sunday, the election could set off a chain of events for Merz — already a historically weak leader — that could ultimately lead to his downfall, and it’s unclear whether the chancellor has a coherent strategy for dealing with the fallout.

In the lead-up to the vote, Merz almost seemed to be in a state of denial.

“I’m not speculating today about what will happen the day after [the election],” Merz said in a television interview last Sunday. “We’ll assess the situation in light of the election results, and we’ll do everything we can to prevent Saxony-Anhalt from falling into the hands of the radicals.”

World.title: Ukraine, Poland explore joint FIFA World Cup bid
World.content:
Ukraine already has experience organizing a major tournament with Poland, Bidnyi added, pointing to the men’s Euro 2012 football championship. “It would be very logical to repeat this successful case,” he said, noting that such a bid could also “invite investors’ attention.”

Any proposal would unfold in a dramatically different context from Euro 2012. Russia’s assault has left Ukraine with reconstruction and recovery needs estimated at nearly $588 billion over the next decade — almost three times the country’s projected nominal GDP for 2025 — according to an assessment by the Ukrainian government, the World Bank Group, the European Commission and the United Nations.

Kremlin chief Vladimir Putin’s onslaught also shows no signs of abating, as Russian forces push to occupy Ukraine and bombard major cities across the country almost every night. Addressing the U.N. General Assembly on Sept. 1, Assembly President Annalena Baerbock said there was “no safe space left” in the country and that civilian casualties during the first half of 2026 were 114 percent higher than during the same period in 2024.

The Donbas Arena offers a glimpse into the infrastructure challenges Ukraine would face in hosting another major tournament. The futuristic stadium in Donetsk staged five Euro 2012 matches, but in 2014 Russian-backed separatists seized control of parts of the region and fighting broke out between them and the Ukrainian army. FC Shakhtar Donetsk, the domestic club that played in the stadium, was forced to leave the city and shelling later damaged the arena. The club has never been able to return and now plays its home games in western Ukraine.

The politics behind the cup

The World Cup is frequently staged with political tensions as a backdrop. Russia itself hosted in 2018, years after Putin annexed Crimea and instigated the war in eastern Ukraine. Some Western politicians called on FIFA to strip Russia of its hosting rights, but the tournament went ahead as planned, offering Moscow an opportunity to project an image of normalcy and prestige amid continued criticism of its belligerent foreign policy.

This summer, FIFA’s relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump overshadowed the run-up to the tournament — and exploded during the competition ahead of a knockout match between America and Belgium.

World.title: Germany’s far-right moment hastens EU’s push for €2T budget deal
World.content:
“With four of the five largest EU member states voting in parliamentary or presidential elections, it will be more difficult to reach an agreement, especially if we look at the rise of anti-European populism,” said Siegfried Mureșan, the Parliament’s lead lawmaker on the budget. “Everyone understands the obvious negative consequences of a delayed adoption and entry into force of the MFF [the Multiannual Financial Framework, the seven-year budget].”

Negotiations on the budget — which must be agreed by all 27 governments — have been deadlocked for months. Neither of the two main groups of countries, those that want the EU to have more to spend and those that want it to have less, has seen an advantage in giving ground so far. European Council President António Costa is currently touring capitals in an effort to narrow differences.

“Saxony-Anhalt could really define the fall,” said one of those diplomats involved in the talks. “It will make it clear that it is crucial to get agreement this year. If we don’t get it in December, it can’t be February or March, that will be too close to the French election.”

Ulrich Siegmund, lead candidate of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), attends an AfD-sponsored outing of Simson motorcycle enthusiasts ahead of upcoming state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on July 26, 2026 in Weissenfels, Germany. The AfD is currently leading in polls in state elections scheduled for September 6 by such a wide margin that it could possibly hold a majority in the state parliament. | Jens Schlueter/Getty Images

Brussels is spooked by the prospect of France’s far-right veteran Marine Le Pen winning the country’s presidential election, scheduled to start on April 18, and following through on her campaign pledge to halve France’s contribution to the EU budget, the diplomats and EU officials said.

Macron’s challenge

But while at the European level that adds urgency for France to get a deal before the election, domestic pressures make it more complicated.



Macron, whose far-right opponents are pushing for massive reductions in the country’s own EU contributions, is under pressure to get a deal that won’t worsen Paris’ national economic woes. He is pushing for new EU-wide taxes, known as “own resources,” as a way to pay for the bloc’s priorities without capitals being stuck with the bill themselves. France wants to give Brussels the power to put levies on U.S. digital giants, foreign polluters and online gambling.

“Any agreement without own resources will be a no-go for France,” said an EU official. “We get it.”

World.title: Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella struggle to stay on the same page
World.content:
In positioning himself for a possible campaign, Bardella had tried to soften the National Rally’s image, especially on the economy, in an attempt to appeal to more moderate voters the party will likely need to win next year’s presidential election.

Le Pen is leading the polls in a crowded field, making it likely she will win the first round of the French election and advance to the two-candidate runoff — a feat she has accomplished twice before, only to lose to French President Emmanuel Macron.

Tensions between the two have bubbled just below the surface in the weeks since Le Pen reasserted herself as the party’s presidential standard-bearer.

On the day after the July verdict, Bardella stood stern-faced beside his mentor as she sought to cast their relationship as a partnership, with Le Pen as the candidate for France’s highest office and her protégé as her pick for prime minister, a much less powerful role.

Bardella did not attend a presidential debate last week in which Le Pen doubled down on a campaign promise to roll back a key element of Macron’s pension reform and allow workers to retire at 62.

He had openly questioned that policy earlier this year as part of his campaign to cast himself as a fiscally responsible leader.

World.title: Don’t take the red pills with Trump’s face on them!
World.content:
And yet, some drug dealers have been making ecstasy tablets shaped like the face of the U.S. president (if he were playing the role of an alien in a very early episode of Star Trek. Never mind Breaking Bad, this is Breaking Bad Design).

Anyway, a Dutch drug institute has warned that the pills are potentially lethal and should not be taken “under any circumstances.” Of course, Trump famously doesn’t drink, let alone take drugs. His body is a temple (albeit a temple that’s been turned into a McDonald’s).

As political leaders change, so does the branding drug dealers use. Trump-shaped ecstasy tablets were first seized by authorities in 2017. Before that, Barack Obama’s visage was often used on illegal drugs. Former President Joe Biden was less popular. He did, after all, once try to ban raves, which wouldn’t have gone down well with the ravers who take ecstasy.

Trump’s face isn’t just on narcotics. This week, the U.S. Mint announced that $1 coins bearing his — rather stern, it must be said — face are in circulation to commemorate the nation’s 250th anniversary (they cost $61, in case you’d forgotten there’s a cost-of-living crisis going on).

It’s the first time a living person has appeared on U.S. currency since 1866, when Spencer Clark, who headed the National Currency Bureau, put his own face on a note in what can only be described as a ballsy move — the 19th-century equivalent of those TV adverts featuring the owner of the company.

But however many items Trump gets his face on, legal or otherwise, he has a long way to go before he gets to the level of name recognition enjoyed by French diplomat Jean Nicot de Villemain, who introduced smoking to France (which means he’s basically their national hero). The Nicotiana plant was named in his honor, and it’s from that we get the word nicotine. Nick O’Teen, incidentally, was the name of a supervillain who battled against Superman in the 1980s, and was also the face of a British anti-smoking campaign.

World.title: Meloni beats Berlusconi’s record as prime minister. Here’s what she wants to do next.
World.content:
Berlusconi’s extraordinary endurance rested on his ability to survive electoral defeats, collapsed governments, criminal trials and repeated predictions of his political death. His wealth, television empire and a party constructed around himself gave him resources independent of his popularity at any particular moment.

Meloni lacks those tycoon-style advantages, but she is still only 49 years old, tops the polls and is planning an electoral reform that could make it easier for her to keep her grip on power. Nearly four years after taking office, she towers over her coalition partners without an obvious challenger on the right.

Italo Bocchino, a former conservative parliamentarian and prominent Meloni supporter, predicted her era “will last 30 years” — even if some of those years are in opposition.

Her appeal, he argued, lies in her unfiltered authenticity: She complains in dialect about high heels and needing the toilet at international summits and press conferences, embraces her “fishwife” nickname and is notorious for eye-rolls that betray what she is thinking.

“She is sincere, she is transparent as glass,” he said. Her image as a petite blonde woman, Bocchino argued, also made a leader from Italy’s post-fascist right appear less threatening to wary voters.

On the other side of the political spectrum, Laura Boldrini, a center-left Democratic Party MP and former speaker of the lower house, insisted Meloni had not yet earned the comparison with Berlusconi.

World.title: Two US sailors removed from Thai resort town after drunken brawl
World.content:
Two sailors from a US aircraft carrier making a port call to Thailand were sent back to the ship after a drunken altercation, Thai police said on Friday.

 

Police were alerted to a "small scuffle" involving the sailors in the early hours of Thursday near Pattaya's nightlife hotspot Walking Street, city police chief Colonel Anek Srathongyoo told the AFP news agency.

"The sailors were drunk and they were fighting, making loud noise," he said.

He described the incident as "trivial" and said local residents had only called police to prevent it from escalating.

The unidentified sailors were not charged as "they did not violate any Thai law," Anek said.

The US Navy sent the pair back to the ship, he added.

The USS Abraham Lincoln's arrival has drawn global media interest after reports of deteriorating living conditions on board after more than 280 days at sea.

The USS Abraham Lincoln arrives at the port in Laem Chabang, 2 September, 2026 AP Photo

It has also put the spotlight on Pattaya, a resort popular with foreign tourists with a reputation for its nightlife, including sex tourism.

Authorities launched a crackdown on sex workers ahead of the ship's visit, although they denied it was linked to the sailors' arrival.

The police chief told AFP there had been no other notable incidents since the Lincoln docked, and one Pattaya masseuse said it had been calmer than previous military port calls.

Nattakamol Chartmontri, who has worked in Pattaya for several years, told AFP many of the sailors appeared "young, well-behaved and rule-abiding."

Pattaya businesses had been hoping for a windfall from the visit, which comes during low season, but Nattakamol, 48, said it had so far stayed quiet.

"People on social media are so hyped about (the sailors), but actually, they have not made a significant difference to Pattaya businesses," she said.

American service members of the USS Abraham Lincoln strike group arrive at a hotel in Pattaya, 2 September, 2026 AP Photo

US Democratic lawmakers called for an investigation into conditions on the Lincoln last month following reports of food shortages, broken plumbing and mental health crises, including attempted suicides.

President Donald Trump dismissed the concerns, which have fuelled criticism of his dragging war on Iran, although the Lincoln was replaced in the Middle East by the USS George Washington.

World.title: Volkswagen to cut 100,000 jobs in biggest ever industry shake-up
World.content:
Volkswagen is about to shed one in seven of its workers.

 

The German car giant said on Thursday that management and unions had agreed to cut a further 50,000 jobs by the end of the decade, on top of 50,000 already planned, bringing total losses to 100,000.

"It is essential to systematically align workforce levels with economic realities," the 10-brand group said in a statement.

The firm had approved a plan involving "the reduction of around 50,000 jobs" on top of another 50,000 already agreed, it added.

Hit by US tariffs, patchy demand for electric cars and, above all, fierce competition in and from China, Europe's largest carmaker is in trouble.

The group, which apart from its namesake brand also includes Audi and Porsche, had already agreed to cut about 50,000 jobs worldwide.

The total 100,000 cuts will be the largest restructuring ever carried out in the global automotive industry, amounting to about 15% of the carmaker's staff worldwide.

The cuts eclipse the auto industry's previous record-holders. General Motors cut 74,000 jobs and closed 21 plants in 1991 as it lost ground to Japanese rivals, and cut a further 47,000 jobs globally in 2009 during its financial crisis restructuring.

Ford cut 35,000 jobs and closed five plants in 2002, then targeted tens of thousands more under its "Way Forward" plan later that decade. Volkswagen's 100,000 is now the largest total on record.

Volkswagen further said that management and unions agreed the future of four German plants — in Hannover, Emden, Zwickau and Neckarsulm — could not be assured into the 2030s.

Their closure would mark the first time Volkswagen has shuttered full-scale factories in its home country.

The adoption of the plans by Volkswagen's supervisory board, made up of both labour and shareholder representatives, marks progress in delicate negotiations between the two sides.

"The supervisory board has unanimously approved the executive board's future plan presented today," CEO Oliver Blume said. "This is a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen Group."

Alongside its namesake marque, the group's stable spans Škoda, SEAT and Cupra at the mass-market end, Audi, Bentley, Lamborghini and Ducati at the premium and luxury end, and Porsche as a standalone sports brand.

World.title: Euronews Culture's Film of the Week: 'Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma'
World.content:
“Sex seems so easy for so many people,” a young filmmaker tells her new lover, laying half-naked in a pool of discarded sweet wrappers. “But I've never been able to get there with someone else unless I'm really far away in my head.”

 

This is one of many moments in Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, Jane Schoenbrun's delirious dissection of slasher movies, that captures its absurd yet intimate magic — but also one that serves as a core reminder for viewers: To reach this movie's orgasmic plane, you too must learn to let go.

The story begins with Kris (Hannah Einbinder), an up-and-coming queer director who, after catching the attention of indie studios with her first feature (“Psycho — but told from the perspective of the shower curtain”), has been tasked with reviving an old summer camp slasher series called Camp Miasma.

Camp Miasma’s lore is richly drawn — as shown in a spectacular opening sequence that only the mind of someone raised by scuzzy VHS tapes and their underground fandoms could conjure.

Little Death (Jack Haven), the killer from the film's fictional Camp Miasma franchise. MUBI

Inspired by the likes of Friday the 13th, The Burning and — most prominently — Sleepaway Camp, the fictional franchise stars a masked serial killer known as Little Death (Jack Haven), who rises from a lake to enact vengeance on groups of mean, horny teens after being drowned for being raised as both a boy and a girl.

In 2026, this gender-bending origin story has become “problematic”, but all the more ripe for a progressive, ‘elevated horror’ reboot — externalised metaphors for generational trauma, anyone?

But Kris, who had her sexual awakening while watching the first movie, has other ideas. She wants to sign on its original final girl — a turban-wearing recluse named Billy Presley (Gillian Anderson), whose thick southern drawl and Norma Desmond demeanor seem to ooze through the screen like sweet, sticky honey.

Billy still lives on the grounds of the original camp, and as Kris enters, the world as she knew it collapses into a libidinous lucid dream; a dissociative space caught between media and reality, where scenery becomes painted backdrops, and a casual fried chicken dinner becomes a sensuous montage of smacking lips and dipping sauce.

Schoenbrun has a unique aptitude for this. Their previous two movies within the Screen Trilogy (We’re All Going to the World’s Fair and I Saw the TV Glow) similarly allegorised pop culture, media and digital communities as transformational spaces — world's within a world that reflect our true selves back, like a psychological mirror.

Another recent horror, Backrooms, also did this well. But while the liminal spaces of that movie became metaphors for negative thought patterns, Camp Miasma's meanings aren't so easy to condense.

Hannah Einbinder as Kris, who lives out her Final Girl fantasy in 'Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma'. MUBI / Ryan Plummer Photography

This is perhaps the whole point. While the genre's tropes — including its misogyny and transphobia — are represented with a meticulous layering of potential theories, Schoenbrun ultimately favours feelings over analysis.

As Kris struggles throughout to balance her deep connection to Camp Miasma with the shame she feels about its more harmful elements, Billy reminds her: “It wasn't about cultural depictions of monstrosity or gender trouble or any of that stuff. It was about two very simple things — flesh and fluids."

Within the margins of their two opinions, a more complicated truth exists that can't easily be intellectualised. Billy and Kris's relationship becomes the example of this — not just a love story, but a swirling, hallucinogenic embrace of animalistic urges and their contradictions.

In another particularly tense scene, in which it's implied that Billy was sexually assaulted as a teenager, the mood suddenly switches, melting into a montage of Little Death committing a violent massacre — heads and torsos speared with comic amounts of blood splatter — to the soundtrack of Counting Crows’ ‘A Long December’.

As the camera pulls back, we catch a glimpse of their eyes through a slit in their TV-like helmet, the absurdity of it all letting slip something human again.

While sometimes "what the hell?" inducing, these tonal and stylistic whiplashes are never jarring. Instead, they coalesce into a singular vision that feels at once so deeply personal to the director, yet recognisable — like staring into the windows of a stranger's house and seeing your own objects inside.

"I liked the danger and powerlessness," Billy tells Kris, sharing what lures her to horror. "It's giving in."

In the same way, Camp Miasma is a film that urges you to give in. To run through the woods with it, bloodied and braless — because Little Death is coming, and what else is a Final Girl to do?

Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma is out at select European cinemas now, with a staggered release across the rest of the continent throughout September.

World.title: Workers say AI makes them look more skilled than they are, study finds
World.content:
Office workers have a quiet new advantage and their bosses cannot always see it.

 

Research published on Tuesday by Use.AI, a platform that bundles several large language models into a single subscription, surveyed 9,684 working adults in the US, UK, Canada, the EU and Latin America.

The study found that 52% said AI had made them appear more experienced than they actually are, painting a picture of delivered results running ahead of underlying skill.

Some 64% said they had used AI to complete work they would otherwise have been unable to do independently, while 43% said it had helped them take on responsibilities they did not yet feel qualified to handle.

A further 35% conceded they would struggle to perform parts of their current job without it, and a quarter worried their employer believes they are more capable than they really are.

Managers are indeed often unaware, with 39% of workers saying they had submitted AI-assisted work without mentioning it and 30% had accepted praise for work the technology substantially produced.

Neither necessarily breaks any rule, since most workplaces have no disclosure requirement, but it does mean performance is being judged without knowing how much of it was outsourced.

The consequences reach into career progression as 19% said AI-assisted work had contributed to a promotion.

Should you have to tell your boss?

The obvious remedy, requiring employees to declare when they have used AI, is one the company behind the research does not support in full.

"I do not think companies should require employees to disclose every interaction with AI," Ihor Herasymov, co-founder and CEO of Use.AI, told Euronews.

"That would quickly become impractical as these tools become embedded in everyday software and routine work," Herasymov explained while proposing a narrower test.

"The more useful threshold is whether AI materially shaped the substance of the work. If it generated a significant part of an analysis, recommendation, presentation, code or other consequential output, employees should disclose that assistance."

The intent, he said, should not be to police staff.

"The purpose should not be surveillance. It should give managers enough context to judge both the work and the human contribution to it," Herasymov said while adding that a workable policy "should focus on material AI assistance, verification and accountability, while making clear that the person submitting the work remains responsible for understanding and defending it."

How managers should actually measure performance

None of this establishes that those employees were unqualified, since using AI skillfully is itself a professional skill that is increasingly relevant.

The difficulty is that finished work no longer reveals what it once did about the person who produced it, which matters most when a company is deciding who is ready for more responsibility.

"Finished output still matters, but it is becoming a less complete measure of capability," Herasymov told Euronews.

How managers should actually measure performance in the age of AI AP Illustration / Peter Hamlin

"Employers also need to understand whether someone can explain the reasoning behind their work, detect flaws in an AI-generated answer, make decisions with incomplete information and respond when the technology produces something wrong or unexpected," Herasymov explained.

To this end, the CEO of Use.AI singled out one skill in particular.

"Problem framing is particularly important. Can someone define the right question, challenge an assumption and explain why one course of action is better than another? That is much harder to infer from a polished final output alone," Herasymov stated.

However, few employers have solved performance assessment in the age of AI.

"We do not yet see a settled model for assessing this. Organisations are still working out how AI should change performance and promotion decisions," Herasymov said, adding that "the distinction between what someone can produce with AI and what they actually understand will become much more important in those decisions."

Tool or crutch?

Asked whether the finding that 35% of workers would struggle without AI troubles a company that sells access to it, Herasymov did not dismiss the concern.

"Yes, I think that finding deserves to be taken seriously," he said.

"The concern begins when someone can produce an answer with AI but cannot reliably recognise when that answer is wrong, explain why it is appropriate, or make a sound judgment when the system has no reliable answer. At that point, the relationship starts to look less like augmentation and more like dependency," Herasymov told Euronews.

He framed it as a trade-off rather than a verdict.

"AI can make people faster and extend what they are able to do. But if those gains come with weaker independent judgment, that is a trade-off employers and technology companies should be willing to recognise and address."

Is AI just a tool or can it become a crutch? AP Illustration / Peter Hamlin

However, the technology is not standing still while employers work this out.

According to Ventureburn citing data from METR, a US non-profit that evaluates the impact of AI systems on society, the time it takes for AI autonomy to double has compressed from an eight-month trend to just 4.7 months.

The same compilation records a 1,400% year-on-year increase in AI's autonomous capabilities between early 2025 and early 2026 while access has observably expanded just as quickly.

Downloads of AI tools rose from 15,000 to 11.8 million, a growth of 780 times, while publicly available MCP tools grew 35-fold to around 177,000.

MCP, or Model Context Protocol, is a standard that lets AI assistants plug directly into other applications and data sources, so they can carry out tasks rather than merely describe how to do them. It enables what is commonly referred to as "agentic AI".

That trajectory sharpens the problem the survey identifies. As more of the work happens without a person directing each step, the finished product reveals progressively less about the person who signed their name to it.

World.title: Two trapped workers rescued from hydropower tunnel nine days after Nepal floods
World.content:
Rescuers in Nepal pulled two workers alive from a hydropower tunnel on Friday as emergency teams continued an operation to reach others believed to be trapped inside, officials said.

 

The two men were rescued from the Trishuli 3A tunnel nine days after floods, caused by a glacier collapse, devastated towns and swept away villages in Nepal on 26 August.

Nepalese lawmaker Shri Ram Neupane posted about the second rescue on his Facebook page shortly after army spokesperson Brigadier General Raja Ram Basnet confirmed the first trapped worker’s rescue.

The men were named as Sanjay Shah, 30, a mechanical foreman, and Kabir Maharjan, 45, a mechanical supervisor, by Home Minister Sudan Gurung.

Local television news channels showed images of the first rescued worker covered in mud and being carried from the site on a rescuer’s shoulder.

Officials said both men were in stable condition and were flown to a hospital in the capital Kathmandu.

Soldiers rescue a worker from a tunnel during an ongoing operation at the Trishuli-3A hydropower project in Nepal's Rasuwa district, 4 September, 2026 Nepal Army via AP/Nepal Army via AP

At least 557 workers are missing from the Trishuli 3A hydropower project along the Trishuli River, with about 115 believed to be trapped in the main tunnel, according to the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal.

Officials present at the rescue site said rescuers believe some people may still be alive inside the tunnel.

Nepal’s Communication Minister Bikram Timilsina said officials remain hopeful that more workers will be rescued.

“We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people,” Timilsina wrote on his Facebook page.

About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels, according to local authorities.

Miracle country

Australian rescue expert Arnold Dix, who has advised on multiple tunnel-collapse rescues, has been supporting the operation remotely and is travelling to Nepal to support teams on the ground.

Earlier on Friday, Dix, president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association, said teams at the Trishuli 3A hydropower project believed they had heard a faint response from inside the tunnel.

He said rescuers had called into the tunnel: "Don't worry, we are rescuing you."

"They believe they received a faint response from inside saying, 'hunchha', yes or OK," Dix told the AFP news agency, adding that he was en route to Nepal to join the rescue effort.

"Right now, I'm 'glass three-quarters full'...After a week of 24/7 heartache, we might, just, be back in miracle country," he said.

People salvage their belongings from a building damaged by flash flooding in Nuwakot district of Nepal, 1 September, 2026 AP Photo

Dix said teams had dug through debris blocking the tunnel for 50 to 60 metres (164-196 feet) and had been hoping for a breakthrough at any moment.

Less than an hour later, rescuers pulled the two men to safety.

Rescue teams in Nepal have recovered more than 1,250 bodies, and more than 5,000 are missing, after the gigantic wave triggered by a rock and ice avalanche roared down the China-Nepal border.

China, as of late Wednesday, said 21 people were killed and 541 were missing on the Tibet side of the border.

World.title: Man lived with pig kidney for nine months before human transplant
World.content:
A genetically modified pig kidney kept a 66-year-old man with kidney failure free of dialysis for a record nine months in a first-of-its-kind bridge transplant. That gives hope in a world where the number of people waiting for organ transplants exceeds the number of organs available.

 

According to a new report published in The Lancet, pig kidney transplants could offer a solution for patients facing long waiting times for human kidneys.

The study patient, a 66-year-old living with kidney failure caused by type 2 diabetes who had been on haemodialysis — a medical treatment that uses a special machine to filter waste products, extra fluids, and toxins from the blood when the kidneys fail — for two years before transplantation, received the pig organ in January 2025.

The patient had no available living donor and was listed for deceased-donor kidney transplantation, for which the expected waiting time was over five years.

Based on the Kidney Transplant Decision Tool — a programme that weighs treatment options and waiting times — the estimated probability of receiving the transplant he needed was approximately 9%, whereas the estimated risk of death or removal from the waiting list exceeded 40%.

The pig kidney featured 69 genomic modifications to improve compatibility and safety, and successfully provided dialysis-free support for 271 days.

From pig kidney to human donor

According to the researchers, the transplanted organ started working immediately. Nine months after the transplant, the kidney was removed. The patient did not show any signs of antibodies against human tissue, which would have made it nearly impossible for him to accept a human kidney, or any animal-borne infections.

After the pig kidney started to fail, it was extracted, and the patient successfully received a human kidney transplant from a deceased donor and maintained stable organ function.

He received the human kidney earlier than expected because doctors found a donor organ with the highest possible level of tissue compatibility.

This level of compatibility is, according to the researchers, "uncommon and largely unpredictable", and under standard organ allocation policies, it confers substantial priority.

Related Vatican says Catholics may receive animal organ transplants in new guidelines

Addressing organ shortages

Transplanting genetically engineered pig organs has been proposed as a solution to the organ shortage. However, the first pig kidney transplant into a living person, in 2024, ended after 52 days when the patient died from unrelated heart problems, and no previous studies had documented xenograft — transplant between species — survival beyond two months.

“This case illustrates both the promise and the remaining challenges of clinical kidney xenotransplantation,” the authors wrote.

According to the researchers, these findings suggest that animal organs could serve as a bridge to traditional transplants for patients facing long wait times for human organs.

“The organ shortage is the greatest crisis we have right now in transplantation,” said lead author Leonardo Riella at Mass General Brigham.

"Our vision is that xenotransplantation could help address this gap—initially as a bridge to get patients off dialysis while they wait for a human donor kidney, and potentially, as we establish long-term safety and durability, as a destination therapy in its own right."

Yet, they warn that this is a single patient with no comparison group, and that the outcome reflects careful patient selection and intensive specialist care that may not be available elsewhere.

World.title: Argentina: Milei reignites dispute over Falkland Islands
World.content:
The Argentine leader said that a change in the US position on the Falkland Islands could be coming, which would alter Washington's years-long neutrality on the issue.

Argentine President Javier Milei said the United States' position on the Falkland Islands could be changing.

He added that his country would impose sanctions on any oil companies operating in the British overseas territory.

In a nationally televised speech on Thursday, Milei reiterated Argentina's stance that the Falkland Islands are part of its territory. This move could further escalate the long-standing dispute with Britain over the islands.

The Argentine leader also praised US President Donald Trump's comments regarding the US potentially revisiting its largely neutral position on the Falklands, saying this is a result of his close relationship with Trump.

According to Milei, the US is considering this change in position due to Argentina being a "reliable partner, aligned with Western values" that can be "a valuable ally in the decades to come."

Argentine President Javier Milei (right) praised his relationship with US President Donald Trump [FILE: October 2025] Image: Jonathan Ernst/REUTERS

Milei announced several moves aimed at stopping the Sea Lion oil project, which is located about 140 miles from the islands — an area that Argentina considers its own. Two companies, one from the UK and one from Israel, plan to begin drilling in the area in the coming months with the goal of producing oil by 2028.

"Argentina will not stand idly by," Milei said, adding that any further advance on the Islands will be viewed as a "violation of our national security."

The Falklands issue is a point of consensus in an Argentine society divided by political differences in other areas.

Britain 'unwavering' position unchanged

Meanwhile, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham's spokesperson said the British government's position was "long-standing and unwavering."

"Sovereignty rests with the UK, and the islanders' right to self-determination is paramount,” he said.

Any change in the US' neutral approach towards the dispute between Britain and Argentina would be a major shift and could contribute to further deterioration in already strained transatlantic relations.

Asked about whether his administration could change its position on the Falkland Islands, Trump said he "always" reviews positions.

"That's just one of many," he added.

In another interview, Trump was asked whether the US would come to help Britain should it be involved in an armed conflict over the islands.

"Your country was not there to help me," he answered, referring to Britain's refusal to take an active part in the joint US-Israeli campaign against Iran.

World.title: FIFA accuses UEFA of 'smear campaign' against Infantino
World.content:
The dispute between the two football associations reached a US court, in which UEFA is looking for permission to collect evidence for criminal proceedings in Switzerland.

World football governing body FIFA took a lash at Europe's UEFA for starting a "smear campaign" and "fishing expedition" against FIFA and its President Gianni Infantino.

This comes after a dispute between the two organizations due to FIFA's plan to sell a stake in its commercial rights, with UEFA submitting an ex parte application to the US District Court in New York to obtain testimony and documents from US-based entities. These documents will be used in potential criminal proceedings in Switzerland, where both FIFA and UEFA are based.

"While these applications are styled as legal pleadings with captions and docket numbers, they are little more than press releases in further support of UEFA’s smear campaign against FIFA and its leadership,” FIFA said in a filing in US District Court in Colorado on Thursday.

FIFA's filing in Colorado was a motion to intervene, requesting that the discovery process be postponed or dismissed.



Spain won the 2026 FIFA World Cup [FILE: July 2026] Image: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu/picture alliance

According to UEFA, the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), an entity which would have had the commercial rights linked over the FIFA World Cup to investors was developed without adequate consulting FIFA's 211 member associations, as well as FIFA's own governing bodies.

UEFA threatened to boycott the FIFA World Cup should the move go ahead.

The move would have affected both the men's and the women's tournaments.

FIFA argued that the association representing European football had tried to scupper the proposal with a bid to keep European football's dominance as is.

Demands for Infatino's resignation

Pressure has been mounting on both FIFA and its President Gianni Infantino since the FFE plans were made public.

Criticism is mounting over FIFA's now-scrapped plans to sell a stake in the World Cup's commercial rights [FILE: May 2026] Image: Ethan Cairns/ZUMA/IMAGO

This resulted in several countries saying they will not support Infantino's reelection for a fourth term as president in March 2027, when the Swiss-born FIFA boss looks for a fourth term in office.

Aside from UEFA, two other continental confederations demand Infantino's resignation.

Both CONCACAF, representing North and Central America and the Caribbean, and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) voiced their objections to Infantino. Only the South American and African confederations still support him.

UEFA also demanded a "genuinely independent external review" of how the proposal came about.

"FIFA cannot investigate itself and expect the football community to simply accept its conclusions," UEFA said.

World.title: Volkswagen to cut 100,000 jobs by end of decade
World.content:
The company will carry out the biggest job cuts ever seen in the industry. Volkswagen also plans to restructure and invest in research.

German automobile giant Volkswagen announced on Thursday that it would be cutting a total of 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade in what is set to be the biggest restructuring ever seen in the global car industry.

The company said that management and trade unions had approved a plan involving the reduction of a further 50,000 jobs, in addition to 50,000 redundancies already agreed.

"It is essential to systematically align workforce levels with economic realities," read a statement from the multi-brand Volkswagen group which, apart from VW itself, also includes Audi and Porsche.

The total of 100,000 cuts amount to about 15% of Volkswagen staff worldwide. The cull eclipses the 50,000 job cuts General Motors made after it declared bankruptcy in 2009.

Unions and management had publicly rowed before signing off on the plans, with the former accusing the latter of not being honest with the workforce after the figure of 100,000 possible job cuts surfaced in the media before being communicated internally.

'The motor of the entire region'

What's more, Volkswagen also said the long-term future of four major German plants – in Hannover, Emden, Zwickau and Neckarsulm — could not be guaranteed. Their closure would mark the first full-scale shuttering of Volkswagen factories in its home country.

"If this plant really were shut down, you could put a big black spot on the map," one long-term employee in Zwickau, Saxony, told the AFP news agency.

"The plant and the jobs outside it, our suppliers, they're the motor of the entire region."

Caught between US tariffs, Chinese competition and a sluggish growth in demand for electric vehicles, Europe's largest carmaker is in trouble.

Company reforms to drive profitability

However, CEO Oliver Blume insisted that the decision to cut 100,000 jobs sent "a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen Group."

Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume said that the company will take responsibility for its entire workforce, its partners, and industrial jobs worldwide [FILE: March 2026] Image: Julian Stratenschulte/dpa/picture alliance

Volkswagen did not give details as to the timing of the cuts and how they would be distributed across the different regions where it has plants and offices, but the company said its focus will turn to North America and that it is looking to expand exports to the Global South.

The plan also includes a three-digit-billion sum investment over the coming years as VW looks to improve technologically through research and development and become more competitive.

Among the moves is a structural change that should bring about faster decision-making and a cut to the number of businesses and holdings it owns by about one-third.

World.title: Berlin: BER Airport Terminal 1 reopened after security scare
World.content:
Police have given the all-clear at Terminal 1 at Berlin's BER Airport following an earlier security scare and evacuation. The airport said some flights had been delayed but they were trying to avoid any cancelations.

Terminal 1 at Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER) was reopened on Thursday evening following an earlier evacuation due to a security scare.

"The police operation has ended," said an airport spokeswoman.

Federal police, responsible for transportation security in Germany, had evacuated BER Terminal 1 at around 5:45 p.m. after a woman reportedly told security staff at a service point that she had a dangerous substance in her luggage.

"A potential threat from the unidentified substance could not be ruled out," the police spokesperson told the dpa news agency.

Police then gave the all-clear at around 8:45 p.m. and confirmed that nobody had been in danger at any point.

Police initially provided no information as to the nature of the substance in question, with analysis results expected in the coming days.

Berlin: BER operations remain restricted

Despite the all-clear, operations at BER remained restricted on Thursday evening.

"Due to the police operation, we will still be experiencing delays and some cancelations until the end of the day," said the airport spokeswoman.

She advised travelers to double-check the status of their flight before arriving at BER and to keep an eye on the boards while at the airport.

"Flights were not stopped," she insisted, emphasizing that there were only delays.

"Regular operations will resume on Friday."

Various emergency services were in action at the scene as dusk fell on Thursday Image: Michael Ukas/dpa/picture alliance

What did the airport say about departures and arrivals?

The airport had confirmed the incident itself earlier on Thursday but said planes that were already prepared to depart could take off as normal and incoming arrivals could also continue to land.

Passenger processing was "relocated to Terminal 2 to the extent that it's possible," a spokesperson said.

Many but not all flights departing Terminal 1 from around 7 p.m. local time were marked as delayed on the airport's website.

An airport press officer told DW that around 30 flights had been delayed but that they were trying to avoid cancellations by redirecting departures to Terminal 2.

Specialist personnel could be seen in action near the building Image: Michael Ukas/dpa/picture alliance

Trains were also impacted by the operation for a time. The city's S-Bahn train service confirmed disruptions on both lines to airport, while Deutsche Bahn also reported widespread disruptions to regional trains.

BER or the "Willy Brandt Airport" in Schönefeld is Berlin's busiest and Germany's third-busiest airport since it opened in 2020. It also serves as the primary airport for many federal government flights. Some 26 million passengers travel through it each year.

The last comparable security disruption at the airport was in March of this year, when flights were disrupted but because of a potentially suspicious aerial object rather than a suspicious item in the terminal.

Personnel responding to the alert went through decontamination procedures on leaving the building Image: Michael Ukas/dpa/picture alliance

World.title: Israel releases first of 5 Lebanese prisoners
World.content:
Israel has agreed to release five civilians in exchange for Lebanese assistance in locating the bodies of missing Lebanese Jewish leaders killed in the 1980s. Talks aimed at ending the war with Hezbollah remain stalled.

A Lebanese man who had been held prisoner in Israel was released on Thursday, the first such handover since the outbreak of the latest conflict between Israel and Hezbollah six months ago.

The release of prisoner Malek Ghazi was confirmed by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), which facilitated his handover to the Lebanese army in the city of Tyre, Lebanon.

Ghazi is to be first of five Lebanese civilians detained by Israeli forces in southern Lebanon who Israel has agreed to release.

"After their interrogation was completed, it became clear that they are civilians who are not members of any terrorist organization, have not engaged in terrorism, and there is no reason to continue holding them in Israel," read a statement from the office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Lebanese officials told the AFP news agency that the four remaining prisoners are expected to be released on Friday.

Lebanon remains main stumbling block to Israel-US-Iran peace To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Lebanon thanks US for prisoner release efforts

"We will continue working until all our prisoners are released, the fate of the missing is revealed, and a complete Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory is achieved," read a statement from Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, who also thanked the United States for its "efforts exerted in this regard."

In Washington, the US State Department said the releases were the "result of US-led mediation between two legitimate governments" and were finalized during a recent trip to Israel by the US ambassador to Lebanon, Michel Issa.

"We commend the government of Israel and the government of Lebanon for demonstrating good faith through these initial steps, and hope this will serve as the basis for expanded discussions on other civilian issues," added the statement.

Dozens of Lebanese prisoners are believed to be held in Israeli detention centers, including several Hezbollah militants but also a number of civilians and at least one Syrian national, according to a list of more than 30 people compiled by the prisoners' families.

Why did Israel agree to release Lebanese prisoners?

As part of the deal to secure the release of the detained Lebanese civilians, Lebanon has been assisting in the search for the bodies of Lebanese Jewish leaders who Israel says were "abducted and murdered by terrorist organizations" during the Lebanese civil war in the 1980s.

A Lebanese official told the Associated Press that Lebanese authorities were "actively searching for the bodies of the Lebanese Jewish leaders."

The statement from Netanyahu's office described these "field operations" as "significant activity."

Could US-backed Israel-Lebanon deal lead to civil war? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Nevertheless, despite the prisoner release, peace talks remain at an impasse.

In June, Lebanon and Israel signed a US-mediated framework deal under which Israeli forces were to withdraw from southern Lebanon in exchange for the disarmament of Hezbollah. But little progress has been made.

Israel-Lebanon talks remain stalled

The news came as Israeli forces reportedly detained more Lebanese citizens.

Lebanese state media reported that troops had entered the town of Halta in southern Lebanon earlier Thursday and seized three men "after the force surrounded several houses and prevented residents from leaving."

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) did not immediately comment.

"However difficult the negotiation process may seem, we will continue to mobilize all necessary efforts to safeguard Lebanon's rights and the interests of the Lebanese people," said Lebanese Prime Minister Salam ahead of further talks in Rome, Italy, later in September. "Particularly our people in the south."

Hezbollah is not a party to the talks and insists it will not give up its weapons in any area north of southern Lebanon's Litani river.

Israeli officials, meanwhile, have said their forces will not withdraw unless the Iran-backed militia is disarmed throughout Lebanon.

World.title: Indonesia: Thousands fall sick from free school meals
World.content:
Hundreds of new food poisoning cases have been reported this week linked to President Prabowo Subianto's free school lunch program. The costly scheme has been dogged by health concerns and allegations of corruption.

More 1,700 people have contracted food poisoning in Indonesia over the past week after eating free school meals provided by the government as part of a new scheme.

At least 725 pupils and 25 teachers at a school in Lasem on the island of Java complained that they felt unwell on Thursday morning after consuming the free lunch on Wednesday.

"They had diarrhea, they were vomiting, and felt nauseous," said the school's principal. "There was a queue at the bathrooms because two of our toilets are under renovation."

Earlier this week, more than 600 students in Sidoarjo, East Java, were also taken to hospital after eating free lunch meals on Tuesday.

In two other cases on Wednesday, 49 people in the East Java city of Nganjuk and 237 in the West Sumatra region of Agam also fell ill.

Children in Sidoarjo, East Java, were taken to the regional general hospital Image: Suryanto/REUTERS

One lawmaker, Charles Honoris, put the total number of food poisoning cases linked to the free school meals scheme as high as 50,000 since, citing health department data.

"This is a failure of the ⁠system," he said.

What has caused the food poisoning?

The mass outbreaks of food poisoning have been blamed on improper food storage and late delivery of pre-cooked meals.

According to the school principal in Lasem, a food taster found that some of the grilled chicken to be distributed was "slimy" and therefore put aside.

"The kitchen operator said the food was cooked at 3 a.m. and it ​was eaten at noon," she reported.

President Prabowo's free school meals scheme

The $12.94 -billion (€11.13-billion) program, launched in January 2025, is one of President Prabowo Subianto's signature policies, intended to improve nutrition for up to 80 million children as well as pregnant and breastfeeding women.

But the costly scheme has been dogged by allegations of corruption, ​leadership changes and spate of mass food poisoning outbreaks.

It was among the first budget items to be cut back as the Indonesian government moved to counter the economic impact of the war in the Middle East and hundreds of people took to the streets of the capital, Jakarta, last week to call for it to be scrapped entirely.

How Indonesia aims to combat childhood malnutrition To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"This has become a national alarm," said Ubaid Matraji, a researcher at the Indonesian Education Monitoring Network.

"The government cannot continue to treat them as mere statistical figures. Behind every number there is a sick child, a panicked family, and the state's failure to guarantee safe food."

The head of Indonesia's National Nutrition Agency, ⁠which oversees the scheme, told a parliamentary hearing that the food poisoning cases would be ​handled "seriously."

Edited by: Zac Crellin

World.title: Trump's Iran strategy: Could this become a forever war?
World.content:
The US has launched fresh attacks on military targets in Iran. It wants to prevent Tehran rebuilding its destroyed capabilities, but risks triggering a sustained downward spiral of reconstruction followed by new attacks.

US President Donald Trump has given a fairly clear description of what the next phase of the Iran war could look like. The Iranians had tried to rebuild their radar equipment, Trump stated after the most recent wave of US strikes. "We waited until it was almost built, and then we hit it," he said.

On Tuesday, American forces once again attacked several targets in Iran. According to US Central Command (CENTCOM), the targets destroyed included "air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites."

'Mowing the grass'

Iran responded by firing rockets and drones at US facilities in the region. With this, the war moved on to what CENTCOM had indicated just a few days earlier could be the strategy for the next phase.

What strategy will Donald Trump choose to pursue next in the war with Iran? Image: Ken Cedeno/REUTERS

According to the news portal Axios, it was considering limited strikes, at regular intervals if necessary, to prevent Iran from reconstituting its military capabilities in the Strait of Hormuz. An American government representative used a concept from Israeli security policy to describe this idea: He called it "mowing the grass."

The metaphor refers to a strategy that doesn't even attempt to promise that an opponent will be defeated once and for all. It is enough to regularly reduce the enemy's military capabilities to the point where the threat remains manageable. When the grass grows back, you "mow" it again.

Applied to the situation in Iran, this would mean the US keeping an eye on which military capabilities the enemy is reconstituting, and attacking once it crosses a certain threshold.

Successes that won't last

In the past few months, the US has scored some military successes. US forces have significantly reduced Iran's military capabilities in the Strait of Hormuz, and have begun clearing Iranian sea mines.

However, these successes will not last. Tehran is repairing or procuring new radar installations, anti-aircraft positions and anti-ship missiles. US bombs could certainly destroy important Iranian positions with targeted strikes. But the knowledge and the industrial basis of Iranian military technology would remain.

This image issued by US CENTCOM shows a precision strike against an Iranian military target in July 2026 Image: US Central Command/AFP

Reconstruction can therefore be delayed, but not prevented. The US will repeatedly be confronted with the same choice: whether to accept that Tehran is regaining its capabilities, or to attack again and destroy them.

Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, warned as early as April that this development could lead to an "enduring low-intensity conflict punctuated by more intensive interventions."

Trump's belligerent warnings

The fact that the strategy of "mowing the grass" is reaching its limits is also because it was never designed for a war with a state. Israel developed the strategy to combat non-state actors like Hamas.

However, as Yacoubian pointed out in her article, the Israeli academics who initially coined the term warned that if the opponent had "statist characteristics and/or more powerful capabilities, 'mowing the grass' might become an outdated military strategy." This is clearly the case with the Strait of Hormuz.

The US needs to keep the strait reliably open. Iran, on the other hand, only needs to make people believe that the passage remains dangerous. In this way, even a significantly weakened opponent can impose substantial costs on Washington.

Keeping the vital shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz open is a priority for the US Image: Atta Kenare/AFP

Another problem for the US is that, while Washington can determine the intensity of its own attacks, it has no control over Tehran's response. This week, Trump warned Tehran not to launch a retaliatory strike, threatening that Iran would be "totally wiped out as a country" if it did.

Nonetheless, the regime in Tehran immediately fired missiles against American facilities in the region. Jordan alone reported 13 ballistic missiles in its airspace, 10 of which it was able to intercept.

The nuclear question

But Yacoubian believes that repeated American attacks carry a far greater risk. She warns that they may lead Tehran to conclude that "pursuit of a nuclear weapon" is the only way to achieve "lasting deterrence." This suggests that, by attacking Iran, the US and Israel could actually accelerate the precise development they sought to bring under control.

The Natanz nuclear facility in Iran was one of the first sites targeted by the US and Israel Image: Planet Labs

From Washington's perspective, the alternatives available to Trump don't look much better. If the president accepts Iran rebuilding its military strength around the Strait of Hormuz, he risks renewed attacks on shipping and disruption of one of the world's most important energy routes.

The consequences for the global economy are well known. In spite of the upheaval and repeated negotiations, a political agreement between Washington and Tehran has so far failed because of apparently insurmountable differences.

America's next 'forever war'?

For Trump, "mowing the grass" has domestic appeal, in spite of the uncertainty it brings to foreign policy. The US president would be able to avoid occupation, nation building and deploying large numbers of American ground troops.

At the same time, it allows him to distance himself from the so-called "forever wars" he repeatedly accused his predecessors in the White House of pursuing.

Ultimately, though, this supposed way of avoiding a forever war could become one of its own. Yacoubian describes it as a "Sisyphean attrition strategy without end." As long as Washington is not prepared at some point to accept the rebuilding of Iran's capabilities, each successful attack merely creates the justification for the next one.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Norway seizes Russian ship in Svalbard to compensate Ukraine
World.content:
Authorities in Norway have seized a Russian ship, the Professor Molchanov, on a court order sought and obtained by Naftogaz in Ukraine. Russia has protested the move, which stems from its refusal to pay Naftogaz damages.

Norwegian courts have ordered the seizure of a Russian ship in the Arctic to enforce part of a $4.22 billion (roughly €3.6 billion) compensation claim won by Ukrainian state energy firm Naftogaz after Moscow's seizure of its assets in Crimea, which Russia illegally annexed in 2014.

Officials announced that the ship had been stopped from departing the port in the Russian coal mining settlement of Barentsburg in the Svalbard archipelago late on Wednesday.

Svalbard has been Norwegian territory since 1925 but is a demilitarized zone where people from dozens of countries, Russia included, can settle without visas under certain conditions.

Russia's ambassador to Norway said that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels.

Around two thirds of Svalbard is designated as national parks and nature reserves, but the coal mining settlement of Barentsburg is home to about a tenth of the archipelago's population Image: Sergei Malgavko/TASS/picture alliance

What do we know about the Professor Molchanov ship being impounded?

The first group to announce the ship's seizure was Covington, the US law firm representing Naftogaz as it tries to secure the compensation awarded to it by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague in 2023.

Russia had refused to pay the fine plus legal fees and interest amid its ongoing war with Ukraine, and Naftogaz has since begun trying to secure the seizure and forced sale of Russian commercial assets via local courts instead.

"Russia cannot evade ​responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," said Naftogaz acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko.

Covington said it had been tracking the ship, the Professor Molchanov, for months. It said its application was approved on Monday by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court, which ordered Svalbard's governor to ensure the ship stayed in dock once it arrived.

The end of coal mining in Svalbard To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Svalbard governor's office later issued a statement confirming that the ship had been seized and would be held in Svalbard.

"The governor will take care of the crew and passengers on board the vessel in collaboration with Trust Arktikugol," it said, referring to the Russian enterprise (meaning "Arctic Coal") that administers the Barentsburg mining settlement.

Norway's Justice Ministry, meanwhile, said the issue did not directly concern the government in Oslo.

"Russia can demand that ​the district court reassess the case," the Justice ‌Ministry said.

How did Russia respond?

Russia's ambassador to Norway, Nikolai Korchunov, said in a statement on Thursday that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels.

"We insist on the immediate release of the vessel and on ensuring the safety of its passengers and crew," he said.

The Kremlin also summoned Norway's ambassador in Moscow to lodge a formal complaint.

Is Svalbard Russia's real leverage in the Arctic? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Professor Molchanov, a repurposed research vessel, arrived in Barentsburg on Tuesday with a party of Russian scientists, according to a journalist who was accompanying them.

"The seizure has had no impact on the expedition participants or the ship's crew. No one has been arrested. We are all going about our business as usual," Andrei Gorbunov, editor-in-chief of Komsomolskaya Pravda (KP) radio wrote on KP's website.

He said that for the time being, "the Professor Molchanov is simply forbidden from leaving the port of Barentsburg," adding it was unclear how long this would remain the case.

Prior to the war in Ukraine Barentsburg was also home to Ukrainian and other foreign nationals. But most have since left, Ukrainians in particular were told to accept an offer of Russian citizenship or leave. Image: Sergei Malgavko/TASS/picture alliance

What is behind Svalbard's special status, and why is it home to the Barentsburg settlement?

Svalbard is an archipelago well to the north of mainland Norway in the Arctic Circle, sparsely populated and thought to be home to slightly fewer than 3,000 people.

It was a whaling base in the 17th and 18th centuries and became a coal mining site at the beginning of the 20th century.

The territory was recognized as part of Norway in 1925, but only after the 1920 establishment of an international treaty — which nowadays has dozens of signatories — designating the area a demilitarized zone where anybody from a signatory state was permitted to settle and work without a visa, provided they met certain conditions.

The Soviet Union eventually acquired three sites and developed them as company towns: Barentsburg, with a remnant population of around 300 mostly Russian nationals, the nearly-abandoned settlement of Pyramiden, and Grumant, which has been left as a ghost town for decades.

Tourism has become a growth industry on the stark but stunning polar archipelago.

Edited by: Zac Crellin
