World.title: Backpacker Carolina Wilga reveals extraordinary outback survival story
World.content:
Lost in Western Australia's harsh outback, Carolina Wilga dragged herself on metre by metre, fearing she would die as she fought dizziness, a desperate thirst and the dry scrub relentlessly tearing at her body.

The German backpacker has now revealed how she survived 11 nights in freezing conditions, chewing on leaves, plant stems and flowers and sipping water from puddles before being found limping, sunburnt and barefoot by farmer Tania Henley on a remote road.

She has also explained how she crashed her van in a nature reserve, driving through a fence, smashing into a rock, and slamming her head against the side window.

Carolina Wilga's van became bogged when she swerved to avoid a crash. (Supplied: WA Police)

Ms Wilga has just published a book of her extraordinary ordeal called 'Escaping the Outback: My Fight for Survival in the Australian Wilderness'.

At the end of June last year, the then 26-year-old left Perth in her Mitsubishi van and went missing after last being seen at a general store in Beacon, 313 kilometres north-east of Perth.

Lured into the bush

Ms Wilga was driving through a rugged nature reserve 36 kilometres north of the remote town when the accident happened.

She initially only remembered fragments of the crash, but has now written that she swerved to avoid what she thought was an oncoming car.

The backpacker said she slept in her van that night and tried unsuccessfully to free the bogged vehicle.

She wrote that there was a sound that she could not explain which she began following deeper into the bush and away from her van.

Ms Wilga acknowledged it made no sense and sounded irrational, but it was what happened.

Loading...

She found herself wearing only a dress, a linen scarf and no shoes in the icy cold night, unable to remember what had happened to the boots, warm wool sweater and jeans she had been wearing.

As she stumbled through the bush, over tree branches and rocks, her head pounding, she realised in a panic that she was lost.

Condition deteriorates

Ms Wilga wrote how she pulled long green plants out of the soil to chew on, saying they tasted sweet, like lollies, but also dry and grassy with no water.

She found flowers but quickly spat them out again when they tasted bitter.

At one point, she also found the skull and bones of what she thought must have been a wild boar.

A collage of drone photos taken north of Beacon shows the terrain in the area where Ms Wilga went missing. (ABC News: Mitchell Edgar)

Desperately hungry, she said she sucked on a bone to get the marrow, but it tasted rotten and so disgusting she could not eat it.

She described the dust and sand sticking to her legs, scratches all over, ants crawling across her body and stings and itches.

Ms Wilga said she scratched herself bloody from sandfly bites and her tongue became swollen.

Family drove her on

Ms Wilga said she asked herself how bad it would be to die, unable to take it any more.

Soon after rain started falling and she lay on her back to let the drops fall in her mouth.

Rescuer describes moment she discovered lost German backpacker The woman who found missing German backpacker Carolina Wilga by the side of an outback road has describes her rescue as "miraculous".

To stay sane and calm, Ms Wilga wrote she developed a mantra: that she should trust herself and she would be fine.

Knowing the sun set on the west coast in Western Australia, she followed it, and eventually she found a track which led her to a riverbed and puddles of water to drink from.

But Ms Wilga said what really gave her strength to keep going was the thought of her family waiting for her.

She pushed on, her feet badly swollen and cut, her mum urging her on in her head.

Carolina Wilga boards a plane after her incredible rescue in WA's remote Wheatbelt.

And then came the moment she said she knew she would survive — finding a cowpat, shards of glass and a rusty drinking can along a fence line she assumed lined a road.

Emotional rescue

When a car appeared in the distance, she said she stepped into the middle of the outback road and started waving her arms in the air.

It was local farmer Tania Henley, driving her car down the remote Mouroubra Road about 24 kilometres north-west of her stranded van.

Tania Henley found missing German backpacker Carolina Wilga. (ABC News: Rhiannon Shine)

Ms Wilga remembered seeing Ms Henley staring at her, her mouth hanging open.

Ms Henley knew who she was because of the massive search and rescue operation underway to find her.

She said they hugged tightly and Ms Henley told her she was safe.

German backpacker Carolina Wilga leaves hospital in Perth Ms Wilga is discharged from Fiona Stanley Hospital after spending five nights there recovering.

Ms Wilga started sobbing, screaming and crying at the same time.

After her rescue, Ms Wilga said she experienced her first panic attacks about being lost in the bush, and said her biggest trauma had been the feeling of being stuck and unable to free herself from her predicament.

But she said she turned that into a strength, learning to trust and motivate herself, helping her keep going through hunger, thirst, cold, exhaustion and impenetrable landscapes to survive.

Editor's story: Ms Wilga's book is only available in German. The ABC used translation tools and verified the excerpts with a fluent German speaker.

World.title: Breaking: Grazier guilty of murdering neighbours at farm gate, jury finds
World.content:
Darryl Valroy Young, 63, has been found guilty of a triple murder at the gate of his north Queensland cattle station.

Married couple Mervyn and Maree Schwarz and her son Graham Tighe were found shot dead at the gate to Young's Shannonvale Station at Bogie on August 4, 2022.

Maree and Mervyn Schwarz (left) and Graham Tighe were found dead at the gate of the Bogie cattle station in 2022. (Supplied/ABC News)

Prosecutors told the trial that Ross Tighe – Graham Tighe's brother – was also shot in the incident but fled in a vehicle and raised the alarm.

The trial heard that Young believed the family, who were his neighbours, were stealing his cattle and he demanded a meeting at the time and place of the shooting.

Young had pleaded not guilty to three counts of murder and one count of attempted murder.

The jury returned a unanimous guilty verdict on three counts of murder this afternoon after deliberating for 15 hours over three days.

Jurors were unable to reach a verdict on one count of attempted murder.

Justice Christopher Johnstone will now direct them on further deliberation on the charge of attempted murder.

World.title: Breaking: Human remains found in search for man missing since January
World.content:
Human remains have been found during the search for a missing South Australian man who was last seen more than seven months ago.

Police this week renewed ground efforts to find the man who disappeared in January near Port Augusta, saying they held "grave concerns for his safety".

A motorbike that the man, who was aged 39 when he went missing, was seen riding was found abandoned in the area on January 24.

Far North region officer in charge, Superintendent Josh Heinze, said that human remains had been found earlier today, but that police could not yet confirm whether or not they belonged to the missing man.

"It is too early to confirm the identity of the human remains. They will be subject to forensic testing and I hope to have the results in the coming days," he said.

"As soon as the identity of the human remains is confirmed, police will provide a further update."

Police said they had been in contact with the missing man's family to advise that remains had been found.

They said they were not currently treating the matter as suspicious.

In the aftermath of the man's disappearance, emergency services launched what police described as a "significant ground and aerial search" over two weeks that involved a police helicopter and drones, as well as the State Emergency Service (SES).

That search led police to consider other nearby areas, and emergency services returned to the area this week.

Superintendent Heinze said the missing man was last seen in Port Augusta West on January 23 and that his motorbike was found the following day around Yorkeys Crossing.

He said police were notified of his disappearance in the following week, and that the human remains were found "a number of kilometres" from the location of the motorbike.

World.title: Fancy cars and hanging with mum, the paradox of Aussie's EPL teen dream
World.content:
Lucas Herrington has gone to number one with a bullet in 2026, at a speed so dizzying it would leave many teenagers' heads spinning.

Turning 19 this weekend, he is fresh off a breakthrough World Cup, has a multi-million-dollar contract in the best football league in the world, and has fans fawning over him.

But true to his persona on the pitch, the central defender is calm, level-headed and capable of tackling any challenge.

"My parents have always instilled that factor of humility in my life and having that humbleness to stay grounded and just to keep working hard," he told Australian media on a call from Hull.

"I'm always trying to get better. So I think it's always having that positive mindset that I've still got a lot of things to work on. And I'm not the finished product."

Herrington was one of Australia's best players throughout the recent World Cup. (Stefan Koops/EYE4IMAGES/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Herrington made his bolt-from-the-blue Socceroos debut in March, which turned into a maiden World Cup appearance a few months later.

His impressive efforts in North America captured interest from some of the biggest clubs in the world including Barcelona and Liverpool.

But he settled on Hull City, newly promoted in the English Premier League, and a five-year deal for a transfer fee reportedly worth $33 million with add-ons, to become the most expensive Australian player ever.

Alessandro Circati recently joined that rich list with his transfer from Parma to Benfica.

Herrington with his manager, Buddy Farah, after signing his record deal with Hull City last month. (Supplied: Hull City)

The money is astronomical for an Australian footballer, and despite his down-to-earth nature, even Herrington was lured in by the EPL stereotype of fancy, fast cars.

"It's a nice car park. I do have a car right now; it's nice. I'm enjoying it," he laughed, almost sheepishly.

But when he speaks about his off-field highlights in his few weeks in England, the teenager goes back to keeping it real.

"Mum's here at the moment. She leaves soon, so I've just been exploring around with her," he said.

"So that's been really nice, some great quality time with her."

Advice from a legend

Herrington made his debut for the Tigers off the bench in their upset win over Manchester United.

"It was only a week and a couple of days from when I landed to that game against Man United," he said.

"Great moment for the city and for me personally, with my mum and my agent in the stands, it was a super proud moment for me.

"And it was a great match, very grateful for the opportunity to be there."

Herrington celebrated the Tigers' upset win over Manchester United to open their season. (Getty Images: Molly Darlington)

He was again used as a substitute in a win over Coventry, while he started the EFL Cup penalty shootout win against Stoke.

A strong show of confidence for the youngster, who is the only Australian in England's top flight.

"It's probably the best league in the world. So to be here at 18 is super special," he said.

"I've always wanted to play in the Premier League, so I'm very grateful for the opportunity from the coaching staff and the club to do so. And I've loved my first three or so weeks here.

"It's a league with the best players in the world, so to be up against them every week is really special and a great challenge for me as a young defender.

"It's just about trying to learn as much as possible from the older boys in the team and just try and take every game as a lesson."

And don't mistake his modesty for meekness; he knows he belongs.

A message reinforced by former Sweden international Zlatan Ibrahimović, who publicly supported Herrington after missing a penalty in the Socceroos' World Cup round of 32 shootout loss to Egypt.

Herrington received plenty of public support after Australia exited the World Cup. (Getty Images: Alex Slitz)

“This is just the beginning of your career," Ibrahimović said on Fox Sports USA's post-game analysis.

"You stepping up there, you show a lot of courage. Not everybody would do that. My friend, you're the best. Don't listen to the rest. Listen, Herrington, if you want to reach out, I'm here."

Ibrahimović made good on his promise and ended up calling the Queensland product himself.

"He just said, really don't fear anyone. I'm here for a reason, so just go enjoy," Herrington said.

Dreams do come true

Herrington's meteoric rise means he has not yet played for Australia in his home state.

Herrington is hoping to play in the Socceroos' upcoming friendlies against Brazil in Queensland. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Something the former Roar product hopes to do in the Socceroos' friendlies against Brazil later this month, in Townsville and Brisbane.

"It'd be a dream come true to play for the Socceroos in Brisbane," he said.

"Something that I've always wanted to do, and to play in front of hopefully a packed-out Suncorp would be a dream, and in front of my family and friends would be awesome."

And he is happy to be a role model for others.

"Just trying to be an inspiration for all the young Australians that there is really a pathway to the Premier League," he said.

"I think a lot of young footballers in Australia like me wake up at all hours in the morning to watch the Premier League.

"So hopefully I can make them proud, make Australia proud.

"Just to keep working hard, enjoy the process, and to have big dreams because dreams do come true."

World.title: Authorities confirm bird flu in fox and suspected case in dolphin
World.content:
H5 bird flu has been detected in a fox in Victoria's south-west, in the state's first recorded case in mammals, authorities say.

Authorities also suspect a dolphin found dead at Lorne died of the virus.

Acting chief veterinary officer Cameron Gunn said the infected fox was found dead on Victoria's Surf Coast.

"We have now confirmed H5 bird flu in a red fox recently found at Torquay collected through our ongoing surveillance and monitoring effort," Dr Gunn said.

Authorities suspect a dolphin died from bird flu off Victoria's south-west coast. (Supplied: South Coast Cetaceans)

But authorities are not concerned about foxes spreading the disease.

"Wild foxes and other scavenging pests have not generally been shown to spread the actual virus when they become infected," Dr Gunn said.

The greater risk was of foxes moving infected carcasses around, he said.

Victoria has recorded 212 positive cases in birds from a total of 892 investigations conducted since June 20.

Victorian authorities have detected H5 bird flu in numerous species, including greater crested terns, magpies and little penguins.

A little penguin on Phillip Island died from the virus last month and the state is in the process of vaccinating the colony.

Little Penguins at Phillip Island are being vaccinated against bird flu. (Supplied: Phillip Island Nature Parks)

Breeding season risk

The discovery of the dead dolphin at Lorne comes a week after the death of a dolphin on South Australia's Fleurieu Peninsula from H5 bird flu.

Victorian chief biodiversity officer James Todd said detections in seals and dolphins were not unexpected, and the virus was expected to spread to new species and other parts of Victoria.

"Particularly as we head into the spring breeding season, where large numbers of birds typically flock and aggregate around, for example, coastal estuaries and inland waterways and wetlands," Dr Todd said.

As a result, the government was focusing its surveillance on areas deemed high-risk, including the Mornington Peninsula, Port Phillip Bay, Western Port Bay and the Gippsland Lakes.

Bird flu has been found in many dead crested terns along Victoria's south-west coastline. (ABC News: Jean Bell)

Vaccinations results

A dead bird found on Sydney's northern beaches last week has been confirmed as the city's first case of H5 bird flu, bringing NSW's total to 20.

Wildlife advocacy group Birdlife Australia said it was concerned about the virus's effect on endangered species.

Birdlife Australia senior public relations adviser Sean Dooley said the virus could spread "quite rapidly" and he was most concerned about it spreading to breeding colonies of endangered species.

NSW announced a vaccination program in August, and the Victorian government has vaccinated about 1,000 little penguins.

Dr Todd said the vaccinated penguins on Phillip Island and at St Kilda Pier had shown an immune response and no adverse impacts.

"Of course, we know that vaccination is not a silver bullet," he said.

"It is a tool that can be used in targeted situations, mostly for captive populations and highly managed and well-studied wild populations like little penguins at Phillip Island and St Kilda."

Threatened species held by Zoos Victoria and other wildlife centres would be prioritised for vaccination, he said.

But he warned Australia was still at the beginning of the spread of the virus and people should expect that wildlife would continue to suffer and die.

"Overseas experience shows that wildlife or impacted wildlife populations can recover from H5 [bird flu] and they can adapt and in some cases they can also build natural immunity," Dr Todd said.

"But it's also observed from overseas that the virus can continue to impact on populations even at a time when they might be starting to recover."

World.title: Tigers coach defends Luai amid 'irrelevant' criticism over PNG trip
World.content:
Benji Marshall insists Jarome Luai is entitled to spend his downtime as he pleases, dismissing "irrelevant" criticism of the Wests Tigers star's recent trip to PNG.

When Luai asked to change his flight out of Townsville following last week's loss to North Queensland, Marshall was unaware his star player would be travelling to his future home country to attend a golf tournament.

The trip came only days after Pepsi unveiled Luai as a brand ambassador ahead of his arrival at the Chiefs for their first NRL season in 2028.

Luai's trip to Port Moresby, and the first of what is likely to be many promotional opportunities with PNG brands, come while he remains on a seven-figure salary with the Tigers.

Loading Instagram content

The five-eighth will also join Parramatta on a one-year deal before his first pre-season with the Chiefs, which begins in more than a year.

Marshall described media concerns over the optics of Luai's enthusiastic PNG links as "irrelevant to me".

"He paid to change his flights [from Townsville] and not come back with us, which happens quite often with players," Marshall said.

"From my opinion, it's his time off.

"What he chooses to do in his time off, that's up to him. In one week's time, he's not going to be here anymore and we're not going to have to worry about any of those things."

In signing Jarome Luai, Papua New Guinea's power has become real Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

Marshall said, in time, Luai's move to the Chiefs could help transform him from villain to hero in the public's eye.

"He always gets painted as the villain for some reason," Marshall said.

"But he's about to walk into a country in about 12 months' time where he's about to be the hero, so it's going to change for him."

Four-time premiership winner Luai arrived at the Tigers last year with hopes of finally reinvigorating the long-struggling joint venture.

Instead, Luai's decision to sign with the Chiefs coincided with a sharp downturn in form that consigned the Tigers to a 15th consecutive year out of finals.

Marshall previously admitted he had let the saga become a distraction for the 15th-placed Tigers, who had been in the top four when Luai signed with the Chiefs.

Benji Marshall (pictured) has no problems with Luai spending time in Papua New Guinea in his downtime. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

"There's obviously a lot of things probably both sides wish went a little bit better, but we are where we are and we've got to move forward," Marshall said.

Marshall still believed Luai's signing was a success for the Tigers, who face top-two side Penrith in their last game of the season.

"There's no regrets from our side about bringing him here whatsoever because he did the job we needed him to," he said.

"I'm sure a lot of people probably have their opinions about what he hasn't done here, but all I've seen are the things he has done here and the impact he has had on the club.

"I'm sure he would admit himself that he would have liked to have contributed more on field performance-wise but all in all, he'll leave here having had an impact on our club."

World.title: Sitting in court with Molly Ticehurst's killer 'extremely confronting'
World.content:
A friend of murdered childcare worker Molly Ticehurst said sitting in the same room as her killer has been "extremely confronting".

Daniel Billings has pleaded guilty to murdering the 28-year-old mother of one in the NSW Central West town of Forbes on the night April 21, 2024.

He was on bail for other charges against Ms Ticehurst, including four counts of sexual assault, when he broke into her bedroom window late on a Sunday night and stabbed her more than a dozen times.

During the second day of his sentence hearing, the Supreme Court in Orange heard Billings had an "obsessive fixation" over how rape allegations made by his ex-partner would impact his future.

The sexual assault charges were discontinued in November 2025 when he pleaded guilty to murder.

Aidan Clarke said it had been "distressing" to be so near to his childhood friend's killer and watch lengthy videos recorded by Billings in the lead-up to and after the murder that were played in court.

"In Australia, hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of people do suffer from mental illness and they wake up every day and don’t murder someone," Mr Clarke said outside court.

Daniel Billings pleaded guilty to murdering Molly Ticehurst. (Supplied)

Billings's mental state examined

On Thursday the defence's forensic psychiatrist Dr Olav Nielssen concluded that Billings's severe depression amounted to a form of impairment that affected his perception of events.

Today the crown's forensic psychiatrist Dr David Greenberg said the murder was more strongly linked to Billings's anger towards Ms Ticehurst.

"He's very angry because he feels he's been slighted," he said.

"He may be ruminating because he's obsessed with the victim.

The 28-year-old was a childcare worker in Forbes. (Supplied )

"I'm not dismissing his depression because [it was] a significant issue ... but there is other information that suggests there are other factors involved."

Dr Greenberg told the court the context of six months of domestic violence and coercive control was significant.

He said the offender's multiple threats of suicide were made in the context of domestic violence, and that Billings planned to kill Ms Ticehurst in a murder-suicide.

"It's not an isolated depression and suicide, this is the context of murder and suicide," he said.

"[It] was certainly something that he referred to on more than one occasion.

Daniel Billings arrived at the Orange courthouse in a Corrective Services van on Friday, surrounded by media. (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

"We can speculate about whether [suicide threats] were related to his depression, but in my opinion ... it may be related to his anger towards the deceased," he told the court.

Defence barrister Sarah Talbert told the court it was the allegation of sexual assault that caused the offender's "catastrophic and tragic escalation".

"That is primarily linked to his hopelessness ... despair and nihilism about the effects of the allegations on his life," she said.

"There is an obsessive fixation ... since he's been arrested for those allegations and what they would mean for his future."

Justice Natalie Adams told the court the sentence will "boil down to" finding whether his depressive illness contributed to the commission of the offence in a material way.

"Is it your finding that it may have contributed but not in a material way?" Justice Adams asked crown prosecutor Lee Carr SC.

"Yes, that's the crown's position," Mr Carr said.

Letter of remorse released

Justice Adams will hand down a sentence next week, and told the court there were no cases where a sentence has not been reduced for an offender who has pleaded guilty.

Supporters of Molly Ticehurst walking into the Orange Supreme Court on Friday. (ABC News: Hamish Cole)

Court documents which have been released during the sentence hearing include an apology letter written by Billings in April 2026.

"How do I feel for what I done? I feel horrible, ashamed, I've ruined so many lives," the letter read.

The New South Wales government reformed its bail legislation in the wake of her death which is colloquially called 'Molly's Law.'

The changes meant alleged offenders on bail for serious domestic violence offences must wear an ankle monitor, and convince a judge why they should be bailed in the first place.

World.title: Everyone is asking the same question about Dom Perrottet. The ICAC just answered it
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsNSWOperation Rosny Everyone is asking the same question about Dom Perrottet. The ICAC just answered it Bevan Shields September 4, 2026 — 4:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The commissioner presiding over the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s Operation Rosny just resolved the question everyone has been pondering: could this saga land Dominic Perrottet in trouble? The answer, Fabian Gleeson, SC, confirmed on Friday, is a very clear “no”. Former premier Dominic Perrottet. James Brickwood For six weeks now, the ugly reality of the NSW Liberal Party’s factional warfare has been exposed for all to see. It’s not a pretty picture. Two key operatives being investigated by the ICAC are the former premier’s younger brothers, Charles and Jean-Claude Perrottet. The claims against those two are incredibly serious. Jean-Claude was allegedly involved in a scheme to rort the state’s donations laws. Charles, a BP executive and “muscle” of the party’s hard-right faction for many years, stands accused of sharing in a $2 million bribe by fugitive Sydney property developer Jean Nassif.



The ICAC heard this week how Charles sought to damage cabinet minister David Elliott – a nemesis of the conservative faction – and remove the then building commissioner David Chandler from office. The brothers deny they have done anything wrong. Perrottet became premier in October 2021 following Gladys Berejiklian’s political demise. He now lives in the US and is a senior executive at BHP. Loading He is largely estranged from Jean-Claude and Charles, has never been named as a person of interest by the commission, has not been called to give evidence, is not accused of wrongdoing, and even referred early rumours about misconduct within his party to the ICAC in 2022. Despite all this, his reputation has been in question amid the spectre of Operation Rosny. Some have been watching the public hearings, waiting and hoping that damaging material might emerge about the former premier. It has not arrived – and is not going to.



On Friday, Charles Perrottet was asked a series of direct questions about whether he ever lobbied his brother to make decisions that might benefit Nassif. He said no. He also denied influencing the then-fair trading minister Eleni Petinos to dump Chandler as building commissioner. At this point, the commissioner jumped in. “I’ll just indicate for the transcript that neither Eleni Petinos nor Dominic Perrottet is a person of interest in this inquiry,” Gleeson said. The former NSW Court of Appeal judge has been measured in his commentary and interventions during hearings. He intervenes only when necessary, and for impact. That makes his decision to state publicly for the first time that the ICAC has no interest in Perrottet more significant than just a passing reference. Charles Perrottet outside the ICAC on Friday. Louie Douvis The ICAC faced criticism last month for allowing an unfounded theory to be aired from the witness box that Perrottet’s decision to move David Elliott from the police portfolio was motivated to benefit Nassif. The theory – which the ICAC did not properly test or repudiate, and is easy to disprove – understandably annoyed Perrottet’s supporters.



There is no doubt Perrottet would have known Jean-Claude and Charles were working to build the influence of the party’s right faction. But that is a long way short from ever being told about anything approaching misconduct, or making decisions in government to aid the agenda of his brothers. Related Article Operation Rosny ‘I did not think it was bogus’: Charles Perrottet did not report extortion attempt to police The ICAC’s challenge over recent weeks has been sorting fact from fiction, particularly when it comes to Nassif and the various claims the Toplace developer made about his influence over the Coalition government. On Friday, it heard telephone intercepts in which Nassif boasted to a friend that Dominic Perrottet was his “boy”. In another call, he says of Perrottet: “The premier is my best friend … They’re my friends and my boys.” Nassif, a renowned bullshit artist and big-noter, was clearly on another planet. The former premier has told friends over recent weeks he never met or spoke with the developer.

World.title: ‘First of many’: Bird flu detected in Sydney’s northern beaches
World.content:
The deadly strain of bird flu that has devastated wildlife around the world has arrived in Sydney, after testing confirmed the virus in a dead greater crested tern found at Warriewood in the northern beaches last week. There were also new detections of H5N1 bird flu in a Hutton’s shearwater in Coffs Harbour, the state’s first case in the endangered species, and a greater crested tern in Port Kembla. H5 bird flu was confirmed in a crested tern found on Sydney’s northern beaches. Neil Bowman More than 20 cases have been detected in NSW by the government’s latest count, while the federal government counts 468 “events” – which can include multiple cases – across Australia. The greater crested tern was found on Friday, August 28. Testing has since confirmed it was carrying bird flu. Northern Beaches Mayor Sue Heins said she suspected it would be “the first of many”.



“We brace ourselves for [bird flu’s] potentially devastating impacts,” she said. Related Article Bird flu ‘Just the beginning’: First mass deaths from H5N1 bird flu confirmed Mammals can contract the virus – and it has so far spread to seals and dolphins and a red fox in other states – but there has been no mammal-to-mammal transmission globally, and the risk to human health is considered low. H5N1 arrived in Australia in June through seabirds blown off course from the sub-Antarctic flyway, having previously spread to every other continent on Earth, wiping out huge numbers of birds and marine mammals. In Australia, the federal government has identified more than 100 species at risk of extinction, and is rolling out a limited number of vaccines to rare and vulnerable birds via the states. In NSW, little penguins in Manly and Barunguba Montague Island are among the wild bird species targeted for vaccination.



Last week, the Australian Antarctic Division announced it intended to temporarily evacuate Macquarie Island, a Southern Ocean research station operated since 1948, because of the psychological risk to staff of living amid large numbers of dying animals in the likely event of a mass mortality on the island. On Heard and McDonald Islands, another Australian territory in the Southern Ocean, the virus has killed large numbers of king and gentoo penguins and about 13,000 of the 17,000 elephant seal pups on Heard Island since October last year. Manly’s little penguins are being targeted for vaccination. Sitthixay Ditthavong Bird flu has not been detected in commercial poultry flocks or captive birds in Australia yet, though it has had severe consequences overseas. In the US, more than 170 million birds have been culled since 2022 and egg prices tripled by 2025. H5N1 also had a significant, although less severe, impact in Britain, where about 5 million chickens were culled and egg prices spiked by about 50 per cent. The NSW government has urged owners of backyard chickens or pet birds to keep them separate from wild birds and keep their food and water undercover.



NSW Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty said there had been no mass mortality or poultry bird events. Related Article Updated

Bird flu ‘Psychological risk to staff’: Looming mass mortality threat on Macquarie Island prompts evacuation “Our focus is on preparedness, surveillance and responding to events quickly,” she said in a statement. “Now is the time for everyone who has backyard chickens or pet birds in aviaries to take precautionary steps to ensure there are no interactions between their chooks and pets with wild birds.” Moriarty also recommended using caution when walking on beaches or parks, ensuring they don’t eat carcasses or chase wild birds: “There is low risk of exposure but it’s important to minimise any risk for your pets.” NSW Health Minister Ryan Park urged Sydneysiders to call authorities if they saw a sick or injured bird.



“We need to deal with that bird as quickly and as efficiently as possible,” he said in a press conference. “The message is very clear to the community, especially right now, is that if you see one of these birds, please don’t go and touch it.” Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888. World.title: ASX Runners of the Week: Kaoko Metals, Vanadium Resources & Piche
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears ASX Runners of the Week: Kaoko Metals, Vanadium Resources & Piche Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd September 4, 2026 — 4:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The week kicked off exactly the way nobody wanted. AI videos of the US blowing up Iran’s Kharg Island littered President Trump’s social media, welcoming pundits to a mad market on Monday. This week’s Bulls N’ Bears ASX Runner of the Week is… Kaoko Metals. The orange leader of the free world was doing his best to unhinge traders, as they immediately did what traders do best — panic about oil. Brent crude flew to as high as US$97.5 a barrel, up over 8 per cent on the week, as attacks were renewed. As if a near triple-digit oil price wasn’t enough, newly appointed Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh used the annual Jackson Hole gathering to remind markets that inflation remains public enemy number one. His hawkish commentary did little to dampen expectations of a September rate hike and as oil moved higher, the teetering bond yields followed.



The bigger concern in bonds, however, may be lurking beneath the surface. Financial markets are increasingly being asked to digest two borrowing binges simultaneously. Washington continues to issue debt like there’s no tomorrow, while the AI arms race has triggered an unprecedented wave of corporate borrowing. More than US$1 trillion (A$1.4 trillion) of corporate debt has now been issued to hyperscalers such as Google, Amazon and Meta as they race to build out infrastructure, a number that, remarkably, is double what it was at just the start of this year! For the first time in years, corporate debt is beginning to compete directly with government bonds for investor capital. The UK’s bond market is already showing signs of strain, trading at its weakest levels since the GFC, while long-dated US Treasury yields continue creeping higher despite increasingly desperate efforts to keep them under control. Last week’s decision by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to double buybacks of long-term government bonds looked suspiciously like an acknowledgement that the debt market is hovering just above the abyss. Yet even that intervention has failed to stop yields from climbing. Markets are now asking a far more uncomfortable question: if doubling bond purchases doesn’t work, what comes next?



Simultaneously, gold tumbled at the start of the week, dropping from above US$4600 (A$6400) an ounce to below US$4300 (A$5965) by Wednesday as traders braced for higher rates and stickier inflation. Then, on Friday, another Fed member, Governor Christopher Waller, poured cold water on expectations of an imminent rate hike, effectively telling markets they were good to go. The knee-jerk traders completely reversed course – of course – sending markets and gold surging, with the yellow metal charging back above US$4520 (A$6210) an ounce, to cap off an intraweek swing of almost 11 per cent. Resources once again dominated Bulls N’ Bears Runners of the Week list, as a newly listed copper explorer wasted no time announcing its arrival, striking it rich in elephant country. Meanwhile, AI uncertainty, central bank jitters and mounting debt fears sent investors scrambling for the safety of something more valuable in the ground. World.title: Genuine concerns over safety at Sydney’s new airport
World.content:
NationalNSWAviation Editorial Genuine concerns over safety at Sydney’s new airport The Herald's View Editorial September 4, 2026 — 4:12pm

September 4, 2026 — 4:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The city’s newest airport has barely got off the ground, only to have problems at Sydney Airport bring it down to earth with a thump. Western Sydney International Airport’s high-tech air traffic control centre is being kept shut for longer than expected, despite cargo flights operating and passenger flights starting in seven weeks. Western Sydney Airport is grappling with technological challenges. The closures have been imposed to free staff to backfill rosters at Sydney’s Kingsford Smith Airport tower. Staffing problems have been at the centre of an unprecedented number of potential systemic lapses at Sydney, with the Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) investigating six separate incidents that occurred within a month. They include a Qantas aircraft narrowly avoiding a runway collision and a Jetstar Airbus A320 being forced to brake when a Qatar Airways 777 was towed uncomfortably close. The ATSB’s preliminary findings on four incidents are due at month’s end.



An air traffic controller told the Herald’s Matt O’Sullivan and Chris Zappone that the control centre for Western Sydney Airport was now shut for more than half the week, leaving it operating for about 18 hours, from shortly after noon to early the next morning, on four consecutive days. Any aircraft requiring an emergency landing would be unable to use the airport during the shutdowns because of the absence of air traffic control. “When all the incidents went very public at Sydney Airport with the tower staffing, they decided to claw back controllers to Sydney Airport, leaving the roster critically short at WSI. Typical rob-Peter-to-pay-Paul scenario,” he said. The situation has been exacerbated by Western Sydney Airport grappling with technological challenges, with poor-quality digital images beamed from cameras on a tower next to the airport’s 3.7-kilometre runway to air traffic controllers 17 kilometres away at Eastern Creek. As a consequence, aircraft have been kept significantly further apart during landing for safety reasons. The air traffic controllers’ union, Civil Air, played down the implications for the new airport of the lapse in staffing, and Airservices Australia, the government-owned organisation responsible for managing air traffic control operations, said it would “return to 24/7 coverage” of the new airport’s air traffic control before the start of passenger flights on October 25. Airports are highly complex organisations and it is the task of government, regulators and unions to make sure they run smoothly, but it is understandable that there are public concerns after the recent spate of mishaps.



Airservices Australia has had capacity problems since the mass retirement of many controllers in 2021, when COVID shut down the aviation sector. Authorities have had years to prepare for Sydney’s second airport. It can take some 18 months to train an air traffic controller, and five years for staff to perform at high levels, yet we are none the wiser if enough are waiting in the wings. Instead, the air traffic control problems that have plagued Sydney Airport are at risk of being repeated at Western Sydney International Airport, as authorities seemingly adopt a just-in-time strategy more appropriate to manufacturing than aviation. Passengers deserve better. Jordan Baker sends a newsletter to subscribers each week. Sign up to receive her Note from the Editor.

A paedophile caught by detectives investigating accused childcare rapist Joshua Brown pleaded guilty on Friday to dozens of child abuse crimes. Matthew Green, also known as Kaleigh Green, showed little expression during a hearing at Melbourne Magistrates’ Court while entering the guilty plea to child rape, bestiality and possessing a child-like sex doll. Paedophile Matthew Green, also known as Kaleigh Green, on Friday pleaded guilty to dozens of child sexual abuse offences. Green, who now identifies as a woman, appeared remotely from Ravenhall prison and is being held in the Forbes unit, a high-protection unit within the jail. Green pleaded guilty to 36 offences, including child rape, producing and transmitting child abuse material, and performing sexual acts in front of a child.



Related Article Courts Accused paedophile Joshua Brown to admit childcare crimes, court hears The 29-year-old also pleaded guilty to two counts of bestiality and one count of possessing a child-like sex doll. Green, who once worked for a property maintenance company, sat with hands clasped and spent much of the hearing looking downward displaying no emotion. “I plead guilty, your honour,” Green said. Sex crime detectives first arrested Green, from Frankston, in September 2025 as part of the ongoing investigating that uncovered Brown.



Joshua Brown. Marija Ercegovac Green’s offending does not relate to childcare settings, and Brown is not listed as a co-accused. Green is connected to the two men through the police investigation, not the offending itself. A raid on a home in April 2025 eventually led investigators to childcare worker Brown, whose arrest exposed the monumental failures in the state’s child safety systems, and prompted a series of major reforms. Detectives arrested Green four months later, but the arrest was first revealed in March after this masthead successfully applied for an order banning publication of the matter to be lifted. Green was originally charged with 194 charges, but the court heard on Friday that they had been struck out and replaced by the 36 charges.



Charges are often rolled up to combine multiple instances of an offence into a single count when accused people plead guilty. Magistrate Michelle Mykytowycz noted Green’s guilty plea and set a plea hearing in the County Court in March next year. Green attended Frankston South’s Mount Erin Secondary College and graduated in 2015. Green was an avid gamer who frequently live-streamed on platforms including Twitch and YouTube. World.title: Everyone is asking the same question about Dom Perrottet. The ICAC just answered it
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsNSWOperation Rosny Everyone is asking the same question about Dom Perrottet. The ICAC just answered it Bevan Shields September 4, 2026 — 4:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The commissioner presiding over the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s Operation Rosny just resolved the question everyone has been pondering: could this saga land Dominic Perrottet in trouble? The answer, Fabian Gleeson, SC, confirmed on Friday, is a very clear “no”. Former premier Dominic Perrottet. James Brickwood For six weeks now, the ugly reality of the NSW Liberal Party’s factional warfare has been exposed for all to see. It’s not a pretty picture. Two key operatives being investigated by the ICAC are the former premier’s younger brothers, Charles and Jean-Claude Perrottet. The claims against those two are incredibly serious. Jean-Claude was allegedly involved in a scheme to rort the state’s donations laws. Charles, a BP executive and “muscle” of the party’s hard-right faction for many years, stands accused of sharing in a $2 million bribe by fugitive Sydney property developer Jean Nassif.



The ICAC heard this week how Charles sought to damage cabinet minister David Elliott – a nemesis of the conservative faction – and remove the then building commissioner David Chandler from office. The brothers deny they have done anything wrong. Perrottet became premier in October 2021 following Gladys Berejiklian’s political demise. He now lives in the US and is a senior executive at BHP. Loading He is largely estranged from Jean-Claude and Charles, has never been named as a person of interest by the commission, has not been called to give evidence, is not accused of wrongdoing, and even referred early rumours about misconduct within his party to the ICAC in 2022. Despite all this, his reputation has been in question amid the spectre of Operation Rosny. Some have been watching the public hearings, waiting and hoping that damaging material might emerge about the former premier. It has not arrived – and is not going to.



On Friday, Charles Perrottet was asked a series of direct questions about whether he ever lobbied his brother to make decisions that might benefit Nassif. He said no. He also denied influencing the then-fair trading minister Eleni Petinos to dump Chandler as building commissioner. At this point, the commissioner jumped in. “I’ll just indicate for the transcript that neither Eleni Petinos nor Dominic Perrottet is a person of interest in this inquiry,” Gleeson said. The former NSW Court of Appeal judge has been measured in his commentary and interventions during hearings. He intervenes only when necessary, and for impact. That makes his decision to state publicly for the first time that the ICAC has no interest in Perrottet more significant than just a passing reference. Charles Perrottet outside the ICAC on Friday. Louie Douvis The ICAC faced criticism last month for allowing an unfounded theory to be aired from the witness box that Perrottet’s decision to move David Elliott from the police portfolio was motivated to benefit Nassif. The theory – which the ICAC did not properly test or repudiate, and is easy to disprove – understandably annoyed Perrottet’s supporters.



There is no doubt Perrottet would have known Jean-Claude and Charles were working to build the influence of the party’s right faction. But that is a long way short from ever being told about anything approaching misconduct, or making decisions in government to aid the agenda of his brothers. Related Article Operation Rosny ‘I did not think it was bogus’: Charles Perrottet did not report extortion attempt to police The ICAC’s challenge over recent weeks has been sorting fact from fiction, particularly when it comes to Nassif and the various claims the Toplace developer made about his influence over the Coalition government. On Friday, it heard telephone intercepts in which Nassif boasted to a friend that Dominic Perrottet was his “boy”. In another call, he says of Perrottet: “The premier is my best friend … They’re my friends and my boys.” Nassif, a renowned bullshit artist and big-noter, was clearly on another planet. The former premier has told friends over recent weeks he never met or spoke with the developer.

World.title: ‘First of many’: Bird flu detected in Sydney’s northern beaches
World.content:
The deadly strain of bird flu that has devastated wildlife around the world has arrived in Sydney, after testing confirmed the virus in a dead greater crested tern found at Warriewood in the northern beaches last week. There were also new detections of H5N1 bird flu in a Hutton’s shearwater in Coffs Harbour, the state’s first case in the endangered species, and a greater crested tern in Port Kembla. H5 bird flu was confirmed in a crested tern found on Sydney’s northern beaches. Neil Bowman More than 20 cases have been detected in NSW by the government’s latest count, while the federal government counts 468 “events” – which can include multiple cases – across Australia. The greater crested tern was found on Friday, August 28. Testing has since confirmed it was carrying bird flu. Northern Beaches Mayor Sue Heins said she suspected it would be “the first of many”.



“We brace ourselves for [bird flu’s] potentially devastating impacts,” she said. Related Article Bird flu ‘Just the beginning’: First mass deaths from H5N1 bird flu confirmed Mammals can contract the virus – and it has so far spread to seals and dolphins and a red fox in other states – but there has been no mammal-to-mammal transmission globally, and the risk to human health is considered low. H5N1 arrived in Australia in June through seabirds blown off course from the sub-Antarctic flyway, having previously spread to every other continent on Earth, wiping out huge numbers of birds and marine mammals. In Australia, the federal government has identified more than 100 species at risk of extinction, and is rolling out a limited number of vaccines to rare and vulnerable birds via the states. In NSW, little penguins in Manly and Barunguba Montague Island are among the wild bird species targeted for vaccination.



Last week, the Australian Antarctic Division announced it intended to temporarily evacuate Macquarie Island, a Southern Ocean research station operated since 1948, because of the psychological risk to staff of living amid large numbers of dying animals in the likely event of a mass mortality on the island. On Heard and McDonald Islands, another Australian territory in the Southern Ocean, the virus has killed large numbers of king and gentoo penguins and about 13,000 of the 17,000 elephant seal pups on Heard Island since October last year. Manly’s little penguins are being targeted for vaccination. Sitthixay Ditthavong Bird flu has not been detected in commercial poultry flocks or captive birds in Australia yet, though it has had severe consequences overseas. In the US, more than 170 million birds have been culled since 2022 and egg prices tripled by 2025. H5N1 also had a significant, although less severe, impact in Britain, where about 5 million chickens were culled and egg prices spiked by about 50 per cent. The NSW government has urged owners of backyard chickens or pet birds to keep them separate from wild birds and keep their food and water undercover.



NSW Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty said there had been no mass mortality or poultry bird events. Related Article Updated

Bird flu ‘Psychological risk to staff’: Looming mass mortality threat on Macquarie Island prompts evacuation “Our focus is on preparedness, surveillance and responding to events quickly,” she said in a statement. “Now is the time for everyone who has backyard chickens or pet birds in aviaries to take precautionary steps to ensure there are no interactions between their chooks and pets with wild birds.” Moriarty also recommended using caution when walking on beaches or parks, ensuring they don’t eat carcasses or chase wild birds: “There is low risk of exposure but it’s important to minimise any risk for your pets.” NSW Health Minister Ryan Park urged Sydneysiders to call authorities if they saw a sick or injured bird.



“We need to deal with that bird as quickly and as efficiently as possible,” he said in a press conference. “The message is very clear to the community, especially right now, is that if you see one of these birds, please don’t go and touch it.” Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888. The week kicked off exactly the way nobody wanted. AI videos of the US blowing up Iran’s Kharg Island littered President Trump’s social media, welcoming pundits to a mad market on Monday. This week’s Bulls N’ Bears ASX Runner of the Week is… Kaoko Metals. The orange leader of the free world was doing his best to unhinge traders, as they immediately did what traders do best — panic about oil. Brent crude flew to as high as US$97.5 a barrel, up over 8 per cent on the week, as attacks were renewed. As if a near triple-digit oil price wasn’t enough, newly appointed Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh used the annual Jackson Hole gathering to remind markets that inflation remains public enemy number one. His hawkish commentary did little to dampen expectations of a September rate hike and as oil moved higher, the teetering bond yields followed.



The bigger concern in bonds, however, may be lurking beneath the surface. Financial markets are increasingly being asked to digest two borrowing binges simultaneously. Washington continues to issue debt like there’s no tomorrow, while the AI arms race has triggered an unprecedented wave of corporate borrowing. More than US$1 trillion (A$1.4 trillion) of corporate debt has now been issued to hyperscalers such as Google, Amazon and Meta as they race to build out infrastructure, a number that, remarkably, is double what it was at just the start of this year! For the first time in years, corporate debt is beginning to compete directly with government bonds for investor capital. The UK’s bond market is already showing signs of strain, trading at its weakest levels since the GFC, while long-dated US Treasury yields continue creeping higher despite increasingly desperate efforts to keep them under control. Last week’s decision by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to double buybacks of long-term government bonds looked suspiciously like an acknowledgement that the debt market is hovering just above the abyss.
